lessons.title: Use AI Safely Once
lessons.coreQuestion: How can I use an AI assistant without handing over my privacy, voice, or final decision?
lessons.blurb: Make several realistic choices, see what the system is actually doing, and leave with one control rule you can use immediately.

steps.title: AI is already inside ordinary decisions
steps.scenario:
A group chat says school is closed tomorrow. The screenshot looks official, but nobody links the source. Someone asks you to repost it. An AI assistant could rewrite the announcement, explain the screenshot, or confidently tell you it is real—but none of those actions proves the claim. Before learning how a model works, you need a way to keep control of what happens next.

This lesson is not graded. Use made-up examples. Do not enter a real name, school, address, password, private message, health detail, or another person's information.
steps.prompt: What would matter most before you shared the announcement: speed, confidence, or evidence that tomorrow's closure is current? Hold your answer; you will test it next.

steps.title: Choose the kind of control each moment needs
steps.prompt: These are not trivia questions. They are small decisions people make while using AI. Sort each next move by the control it protects; retry any choice without penalty.

items.text: Ask for three possible titles, then choose and rewrite one in your own voice.
Confirm tonight's opening hours on the venue's official page before your friend travels.
Describe an argument without names or screenshots before asking for calmer reply ideas.
Compare several possible plans, then let the people involved make the final choice.
Verify a specific number with a current independent source before acting on it.
Replace a real location and personal details with an invented example before typing.

steps.reveal: You just used three different controls: AI can generate options, outside evidence checks consequential facts, and redaction protects the people inside the prompt.

steps.title: The answer is one part. You are another.
steps.body:
An AI answer is not one clever box that knows things. A few parts do the work, and you are one of them.

The app takes your words. A guesser writes the answer — it is working out which words usually come next, not looking anything up. Sometimes an extra tool is plugged in that can check something real. Then it comes back to you.

Here is the part that matters. If the answer is wrong, the guesser does not pay for it. You do, and so does anyone it affects.

So this lesson is about staying safe before it is about anything technical. A smooth answer is useful material. It is not permission to share something private, and it is not proof that anything in it is true.

The machine writes. You decide.
steps.mistake: Treating it as one clever box that knows everything, and assuming its tidy answer has already done the checking and the deciding for you.
steps.good: Name the job you are giving AI, remove information it does not need, and keep the final check and decision with a person.

steps.title: Context changes the prediction
steps.strong: Write three short ways to tell a close friend I cannot come tonight. Keep the tone warm, do not invent a reason, and leave the final wording for me to choose.
steps.why: The model predicts from the words and context it receives. Clear audience, limits, and purpose change the likely output. Better context improves fit; it still does not make an invented claim true or make the final choice for you.

steps.goal: Use AI to help plan a group meetup without exposing private information or treating a likely answer as a verified plan.

State the goal and limits
Ask for several options
Check current facts independently
Let the people involved decide
choices: Ask for several options
Check current facts independently
Let the people involved decide
Remove private details
State the goal and limits
steps.note: The order matters. Protect people before typing, define the real task, use prediction for options, verify the current details that change the plan, and keep the consequence with the humans involved.

steps.title: Make the whole decision
steps.question: A friend sends you a private group-chat screenshot and asks AI to plan a meetup from it. The answer suggests a venue with exact prices and opening hours. Which complete next move keeps the tool useful without giving it control?

options.text: Paste the screenshot because exact personal context will make the plan more accurate, then follow the most confident answer.
options.feedback: More private context is not automatically safer or necessary, and confidence is not evidence that current venue details are correct.

options.text: Remove names and private details, state the group's real constraints, use AI for options, verify current venue facts, and let the group decide.
options.feedback: That combines privacy, useful context, independent verification, and human decision-making. AI helps without owning the consequence.

options.text: Ask the same AI to cite itself and promise the prices are current before sending the plan to everyone.
options.feedback: A stronger promise from the same system is still not independent evidence. Check the venue's current information outside the chatbot.

options.text: Never use AI for planning because any mistake means the tool is useless.
options.feedback: That avoids the risk by losing the benefit. The stronger skill is deciding what AI can help with and what a person must protect, check, and decide.

lessons.title: What Is Actually Happening
lessons.coreQuestion: When AI gives you an answer, what are the pieces behind it, and which part is still your job?
lessons.blurb: See the few simple parts behind any AI answer, so you always know which part you still decide.

steps.title: The answer came fast. The choice is still yours.
steps.scenario:
You ask an app when the last bus leaves. It says 10:40 p.m.

You need that bus to get home. The screen looks confident. But you cannot tell if it read today's timetable, or if it is repeating something it saw months ago.
steps.prompt: What would you want to know before you plan your night around 10:40?

steps.title: Which part is doing each job?
steps.prompt: Sort each job. Get it wrong as often as you like — the point is to see the parts, not one magic box.

items.text: Decides the goal: get home safely
Shows you the screen you type into
Writes the answer by guessing which words come next
Looks up today's real bus times
Checks the real timetable and decides what to do

steps.reveal: The app is the screen. The guesser writes. A helper can fetch something real. None of those three pays for it if the bus time is wrong. You check, and you decide.

steps.title: Four parts, and you are the last one
steps.body:
An AI answer is not one magic box. It is a few parts working together.

The app is the thing you type into. A website, a keyboard, a chat box, a game.

The guesser is the part that writes the answer. People call it a model. It has read an enormous amount of writing, and it guesses which words should come next. It is guessing, not looking things up.

Helpers are extras the app can plug in: live search, a calculator, your files. Helpers can fetch real, current facts. The guesser on its own cannot.

You are the last part. You read it, check it if it matters, and decide what to do.

Here is why this matters. The guesser sounds exactly the same whether it checked something or not.
steps.mistake: Calling the whole thing 'the AI' and assuming a polished answer means every hidden part worked correctly.
steps.good: Ask which product, model, data, and tools are involved, then keep the final decision with the person affected.

Have the person responsible inspect the output and choose
choices: Have the person responsible inspect the output and choose
Let the model organize the supplied details
Remove the customer's name, phone number, and address
Use a current source or calculator for facts the decision depends on
State the comparison goal and what matters
steps.note: Take private details out before you type. The guesser can lay out the choices. Helpers can add today's real prices. You still make the call.

steps.title: Try it on something new
steps.question: A plant app photographs a leaf and says the plant is safe to eat. Which answer describes what actually happened?

options.text: The app shows the screen, a vision model predicts a match, plant references may supply information, and a qualified person must verify before anyone eats it.
options.feedback: Yes. You separated interface, prediction, possible data, and the human decision at the point where the consequence matters.

options.text: The app recognized the plant, so the model and a trained botanist have effectively made the same decision.
options.feedback: Recognition is a prediction, not professional verification. The consequence is too high to collapse those roles.

options.text: If the product used live search, the answer is current and the human check becomes optional.
options.feedback: Current data can improve an answer without proving the match or removing the need for expert judgment.

options.text: Avoid every photo-identification tool because prediction and search are never useful together.
options.feedback: The tool can help narrow possibilities. The control is matching trust to the consequence, not rejecting useful support.

lessons.title: Change One Clue, Change the Answer
lessons.coreQuestion: Why do the words around your question change the answer, and why can a likely answer still be wrong?
lessons.blurb: Change one clue, watch the answer move, and see why a good guess is not proof.

steps.title: One message, three different endings
steps.scenario:
You start typing: 'I cannot make it tonight because…' Your phone offers to finish it for you.

In the team group chat it offers 'I have a match'. In the family chat it offers 'I feel sick'. In the game chat it offers 'the update is still downloading'.

The start was the same every time. The words around it changed. So the guess changed.
steps.prompt: You are in a chat about a cancelled birthday party. Which ending would your phone offer, and what made you pick it?

steps.title: Which chat does each ending fit?
steps.prompt: Sort each ending by the chat it fits best. More than one could work. Pick the strongest clue.

items.text: …the pan is already smoking.
…the new brake cable arrives on Friday.
…I need a bit of time before we talk.
…the sauce needs ten more minutes.
…my dad said he would pay for the part.
…I do not want this to turn into another argument.

steps.reveal: The AI leans on the words around your question. Change the clues and a different ending fits. That makes the ending more likely. It does not make it true.

steps.title: It builds the answer one word at a time
steps.body:
The part that writes the answer is a guesser. People call it a model.

It has read an enormous amount of writing. Given your words so far, it picks the word that fits best. Then it does that again. And again. That is how a whole answer gets built.

People call this predicting. It only means guessing what comes next.

So the answer arrives one piece at a time. It was never sitting there finished, waiting for you.

Everything around your question is a clue: the earlier messages, the chat you are in, the details you added. People call all those clues together the context.

More clues make the guess fit better. Fitting better is not the same as being right. A homework answer can read beautifully and still be wrong.

This lesson works entirely inside LearningAI. If you do try an outside app, use a made-up example and keep private details out.
steps.mistake: Thinking a smooth paragraph means the AI understands the world the way you do.
steps.good: Use clues to shape the guess, then check the facts yourself before you rely on them.

Pick a made-up half-finished sentence

steps.note: A fair test changes one clue, not five. The evidence is that the ending moved.

steps.title: Try it on something new
steps.question: A chatbot finishes 'The shop is shut because…' one way after you add 'holiday notice', and another way after you add 'broken freezer'. What is the safest thing to conclude?

options.text: The new clue changed which ending fitted. Either ending still needs checking before anyone acts on it.
options.feedback: Yes. Clues change what is likely. Only evidence tells you what is true.

options.text: The second answer is probably true, because it used the newer clue and sounded more exact.
options.feedback: Exact wording is easy to guess. The clue shaped the sentence. It did not check the shop.

options.text: The AI remembered what really happened at that shop and picked the matching ending.
options.feedback: Nothing here shows it knows that shop. It wrote what fitted the clues you gave it.

options.text: Both answers are useless, because a guessed sentence can never help with a real task.
options.feedback: Guessed sentences can be useful. Your job is knowing when a guess needs checking.

lessons.title: A Typo Costs Nothing. This Costs a Lot.
lessons.coreQuestion: If a messy message cannot hurt the machine, what can careless use cost me?
lessons.blurb: Type badly without fear. Guard your private details, your time, your voice, and the final call.

steps.title: The typo is harmless. The screenshot is not.
steps.scenario:
A friend sent you a message and you cannot work out what they meant. You want help writing back.

You worry your question is badly written. So you think about pasting in the whole chat, screenshots and all, to give the AI everything.

The typos cannot hurt the AI. Sharing your friend's messages can hurt your friend.
steps.prompt: Which one actually deserves your worry: the messy wording, the private chat, or both? Say why.

steps.title: Just try again, or stop first?
steps.prompt: Sort what you can safely redo from what needs you to stop and think.

items.text: A half-finished sentence full of spelling mistakes
A screenshot of a friend's chat with names and numbers in it
Changing your mind about what you want after seeing the first draft
Letting AI send a message to someone before you have read it
Asking the same question again in simpler words
Spending an hour hunting the perfect answer instead of just deciding

steps.reveal: You cannot hurt the AI's feelings, and a typo breaks nothing. You can leak someone's private messages, lose an hour, lose your own voice, or act on a wrong answer. Worry about the cost, not the sentence.

steps.title: Keep the mess, remove the exposure
steps.weak: help me answer this im confused [whole screenshot of the chat, with names, numbers and where they live]
steps.strong: help me write 3 replies to [a friend]. [what happened in one line]. Keep it [how I want to sound]. Do not invent reasons for what they did. I will pick one and rewrite it.

steps.title: A redo is free. A consequence is not.
steps.body:
The AI writes an answer from whatever words you give it. A messy question may get a messy answer. You can fix that in your next message. Nothing is lost.

Some things do not undo. Your friend's private chat, once pasted, is out. So is money spent, a message sent in the wrong voice, or a decision made from an invented fact.

So before you paste anything into an outside app, swap things out. Real names, real messages, your school, your address, anything about money or health. Use made-up stand-ins instead.

Everything you need for this lesson is right here. You never have to send a real message anywhere to finish it.
steps.mistake: Polishing your sentence while ignoring whose private details are sitting inside it.
steps.good: Send a rough question with the private parts taken out, then check the answer before you act on it.

steps.title: Get control back after a bad first answer
steps.goal: Fix an answer that missed your point, without starting again and without giving away more private detail.
correct: Say what the answer got wrong
Say what you actually want, in one line
Add the one missing detail that is not private
Ask for a few new versions
Pick one, rewrite it, and decide whether to use it
choices: Ask for a few new versions
Add the one missing detail that is not private
Pick one, rewrite it, and decide whether to use it
Say what you actually want, in one line
Say what the answer got wrong
steps.note: Fixing things is normal. Handing over more private detail is not the price of a better answer.

steps.title: Pick the move you can undo
steps.question: You ask AI to write a listing to sell your old bike. The draft has typos, invents that the brakes are new, and includes your home address. What is the best fix?

options.text: Take out the address, correct the brake claim, ask for a new draft using only true facts, and read it before posting.
options.feedback: Yes. Wording is cheap to redo. Your address, the truth, and the posting are what you guard.

options.text: Fix the typos only, because bad spelling is what puts buyers off most.
options.feedback: A false claim about the brakes and your home address cost far more than a typo does.

options.text: Paste in more personal detail so the AI can get the listing perfect next time.
options.feedback: A better fit does not earn it your private details. Give only the facts about the bike.

options.text: Delete it all and stop using AI, because one bad draft proves it cannot help.
options.feedback: The bad draft costs nothing to redo. Fixing it while holding your boundaries is the real skill.

lessons.title: Check It, Then Decide
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I work out what needs checking, find proof somewhere else, and make the call myself?
lessons.blurb: Turn one confident-sounding answer into a checked decision that you actually own.

steps.title: A confident answer can still send someone the wrong way
steps.scenario:
Your brother has hurt his wrist. Your mum asks you to find out when the walk-in clinic shuts.

An AI says 8 p.m. You would leave at 7:20.

That 8 p.m. could come from an old page, from a live search, or from nothing at all. Asking the AI to sound more sure will not keep the doors open.
steps.prompt: Which exact fact would change what you do, and where could you check it without asking the same AI again?

steps.title: Match the checking to the cost
steps.prompt: Decide how hard each answer needs checking. Not every draft needs an investigation. Not every serious claim can ride on how good it sounds.
buckets: Just read it and use it
AI does not get to decide this

items.text: Three name ideas for a made-up comic character
What time the clinic shuts tonight
Whether a text asking you for a payment is real
Whether someone should stop taking medicine a doctor gave them
A rough first draft of a caption for the team photo
Whether a classmate should be punished for something someone accused them of

steps.reveal: The bigger the cost of being wrong, the harder you check. When health, safety, or someone's name is involved, AI can help you think. It does not get the final say.

steps.title: Build a trail you can show
steps.claim: The clinic shuts at 8 p.m. tonight.
steps: Pick the one fact that changes what you do
Find a source that is actually in charge of that fact
Check the date, the place, and the exact wording
Write down whether it held up, failed, or is still unclear
Decide from the evidence and the cost, not from how sure the AI sounded
steps.note: The clinic's own page or phone line is real proof. Asking the same chatbot 'are you sure?' is not.

steps.title: A useful answer is not proof
steps.body:
The AI writes what fits. Some apps can also run a live search and pull in what they find. Even then, links and quotes need a look. A link can point somewhere that never says what the answer claims.

Checking means testing the claim against something outside that answer. Deciding means weighing what you found against the cost of being wrong, then choosing.

Keep private things out of outside apps. Use a made-up example, or take out names, addresses, account numbers, and health details first.

The claim trail above is enough to finish this lesson on its own.
steps.mistake: Asking the same AI to repeat itself, add links, or sound careful, then calling that proof.
steps.good: Name the fact that matters, check a source that owns it, say honestly how sure you are, and decide yourself.

steps.title: Decide after the check
steps.goal: Deal with a message saying you must pay through a link within one hour or lose your account.
correct: Do not tap the link or type in any account details
Name the claim: this bill is real and it is urgent
Reach the company a way you already know is real
Compare what they say with what the message said
Decide whether to pay, report it, or ignore it
choices: Compare what they say with what the message said
Decide whether to pay, report it, or ignore it
Reach the company a way you already know is real
Do not tap the link or type in any account details
Name the claim: this bill is real and it is urgent
steps.note: Being rushed is a reason to check harder. It is never a reason to skip checking.

steps.title: Use the whole habit
steps.question: An AI says a weekend market lets sellers turn up without booking. Your friend plans to travel two hours with handmade things to sell. Which answer shows the full skill?

options.text: Name booking as the fact that matters. Check the market's own rules, or ask the organiser. Then decide whether the trip is worth it.
options.feedback: Yes. You matched the checking to the cost, and the travel decision stayed with a person.

options.text: Ask the AI for three more versions of the answer and trust the one it repeats most.
options.feedback: The same AI repeating itself is not proof. The organiser owns that rule.

options.text: Go anyway, because the answer gave an exact arrival time, so it probably came from somewhere real.
options.feedback: Exact details are easy to guess. Two hours of travel is worth one check.

options.text: Cancel straight away, because an uncertain answer means the market is a bad idea.
options.feedback: Not knowing is a reason to check. It is not proof that the trip is bad.

lessons.title: Where Did This Come From?
lessons.coreQuestion: When AI makes a picture, some writing, or a voice, how can I tell where it really came from?
lessons.blurb: Learn why you cannot tell how something was made just by looking at it, and what to check instead.

steps.title: It looks real. That tells you nothing.
steps.scenario:
You ask an app for a poster of a glass city under two moons. Seconds later, there it is. It looks incredible.

But you cannot tell how the app got it. It might have made the picture itself. It might have found one someone else drew. It might have mixed both together.
steps.prompt: If a friend asked "did the AI actually make that?", what could you honestly say right now?

steps.title: Made or found, and why you cannot see the difference
steps.body:
There are two different things an app can do, and they look identical on screen.

Made means the AI built something new, piece by piece, from patterns it learned. Nobody drew that exact picture before.

Found means the app went and got something that already existed, that a real person made.

Here is the problem. A finished picture cannot tell you which one happened. Looking closer does not help. Neither does it looking impressive.

The only way to know is if the app tells you. Some apps show a link to where something came from, or a small label saying the AI made this. That label is your evidence. The picture itself never is.

If there is no label and no link, the honest answer is "I do not know where this came from". That is a real answer, and it is the right one.
steps.mistake: Assuming that a surprising result proves the assistant generated every part of it from scratch.
steps.good: Ask what system or tool produced the result, what source information is available, and what still needs human checking.

steps.title: What can you honestly say?
steps.prompt: For each one, pick the strongest thing you are allowed to say. Do not judge by how good it looks.

items.text: The product's activity record says 'image generated' and provides content credentials for this result.
The assistant gives a direct source link to a museum photograph and says it retrieved that exact image.
A strange picture appears with no source, tool label, or creation record.
A quoted paragraph includes a working link to the original article and matches it word for word.
A voice clip sounds like a real person, but there is no label explaining whether it was recorded, cloned, or synthesized.

steps.reveal: Looking good is not evidence. A label or a link tells you where something came from. No label means "I do not know" — and saying that is not a failure.

steps.question: An app gives you a convincing picture of something imaginary. There is no label and no link. What is the most honest thing you can say?

options.text: The origin is unclear. I can describe the result, but I need provenance or source evidence before claiming it was generated or found.
options.feedback: Right. Novelty and appearance do not prove origin. You kept the claim inside the available evidence.

options.text: If it looks good, the origin and consent questions no longer matter.
options.feedback: Quality does not answer who or what was used, whether permission existed, or how an audience may interpret the result.

lessons.title: Sure-Sounding and Still Wrong
lessons.coreQuestion: Why can AI sound totally certain and still be wrong, and what should I do about it?
lessons.blurb: A made-up detail sounds exactly as sure as a true one. You cannot feel the difference. You have to check.

steps.title: The smooth wrong answer
steps.scenario:
You ask an AI about your own town. Back come dates, names and numbers. Smooth, exact, completely sure of itself.

One of those facts is invented. Nothing in the wording gives it away. It reads exactly like the true parts.
steps.prompt: Honest guess before you read on: if the AI were making something up, would it sound less sure?

steps.title: Meet the word: hallucination
steps.body:
When an AI states something false as if it were a fact, people call that a hallucination.

It is not lying. Lying needs someone who means to trick you, and there is nobody in there.

Here is what is really going on. The AI writes by guessing which words fit next, over and over, from patterns in a huge amount of human writing. Its target is to sound right. Whether something is true is a different question, and it has no way to check.

It also has no 'I do not know' light inside. So when it reaches a gap in what it learned, it fills that gap smoothly with whatever fits.

Some apps can now search the web while they answer. That helps. It does not fix this. They still make things up. So you still check.
steps.mistake: Believing an answer because it sounded sure and gave exact numbers.
steps.good: Treating a confident tone as worth nothing. A made-up detail arrives just as smooth, so you check instead of going by feel.

steps.title: Where would you spot the slip?
steps.prompt: You want to catch a made-up fact on purpose. Sort each topic by whether you could check the answer straight away.

items.text: The history of the town you grew up in
A meal you have cooked dozens of times
Your favourite band, and the exact dates their albums came out
A huge topic you barely know, like the history of France
The sport you play, and its exact rules and records
A basic definition anyone could look up in a second

steps.reveal: Narrow, personal topics are where the AI is most tempted to invent, and where you spot it instantly, because you already know. Big general topics are harder: either you cannot tell, or it is easy to get right.

steps.goal: Test a claim you can check, without giving away anyone's private details.

lessons.title: What Its Words Do Not Prove
lessons.coreQuestion: When an AI sounds kind, sure, or close to me, what has it actually proved?
lessons.blurb: Warm words can help, and the feeling is real. Keep what helps without mistaking a written line for a friendship.

steps.title: A helpful sentence can still feel personal
steps.scenario:
Someone types to an assistant: 'I finally finished my project.' It replies: 'I am proud of you. I knew you could do it.'

That might feel good. It might even help. But the words on their own do not prove that anything felt proud, knew them, or has been beside them all term.
steps.prompt: Keep the useful part without pretending it proves a friendship. Rewrite that reply as one honest sentence.

steps.title: Judge it by evidence, not by tone
steps.body:
AI learned patterns from how people write. So it can produce lines that sound warm, sure, funny, worried, or loyal. That style can genuinely help. It can make you stop, think, or feel encouraged. Your reaction is real.

The words still prove nothing about what sits behind them. They do not show that it feels anything, or that it knows you. They do not show that it shares the blame, or replaces a person who cares.

Split it into two questions. Was this reply useful to me? And what can this thing actually do, know, or answer for?

You can answer the first from how it went. For the second, test what it can actually do. Do not go by lines like 'I think', 'I care', or 'I have got your back'.
steps.mistake: Either treating warm words as proof of a friendship, or mocking someone for being moved by them.
steps.good: Admit the effect was real. Turn the claim into something you can test. Take anything about care or safety to a person.

steps.title: What kind of claim is this?
steps.prompt: Sort each line by what kind of claim it is.

items.text: 'I can turn this paragraph into three bullet points.'
'I am proud of you and I will always be here for you.'
'I checked every source and this answer is definitely right.'
'Do not tell anyone. I can get you through this on my own.'
'I know exactly how you feel.'
'I can write you some options, but you should pick which one fits.'

steps.reveal: You can test what it can do: read the bullet points, open the links, compare the options. Feelings and friendship are not proved by words like 'I care'. When something needs real care, trust, or emergency help, bring in a person who can understand it and take responsibility.

steps.why: The stronger reading keeps your real reaction and only claims what the words can back up. It turns a nice-sounding line into something you can use, without confusing it with a person who cares.

lessons.title: Pause Before You Allow It
lessons.coreQuestion: Before I sign in, upload, download, pay, post, or let AI act for me, what should I check?
lessons.blurb: Safety is not one magic word on a page. Check who is asking, what they get, and whether you can undo it.

steps.title: The button is not the decision
steps.scenario:
A link opens a slick AI homework helper. It wants you to sign in with your Google account and let it into your school files. It also wants to install a small extra program and start a free trial.

The page looks professional. There is a little padlock next to the address.

None of that tells you who runs it, or what happens after you tap Allow.
steps.prompt: Before you tap anything, name two things that could happen next. What could this get, change, install, charge, send, or keep?

steps.title: Check what happens, not how the page looks
steps.body:
A page can look safe and still be a trap. A scary warning can show up on a service that is completely fine. So do not decide from how it looks.

Instead, stop before anything that hands over your information or lets something into your accounts. Stop before anything that installs a program, signs you up, posts, sends, or would be hard to undo.

One word first. When an app asks to use your files, your camera, or your account, it is asking for permission. Permission just means you letting it do that. You can usually take it back later in your settings.

Seven things to check:
1. Who is asking?
2. Where is this actually going: which app, which website, whose account?
3. What information does it get to see or keep?
4. What can it look at, change, or send, and for how long?
5. Will it install something, start charging you, post something, or message someone?
6. Can you undo it, cancel it, or take the access back?
7. Can you close the link and reach the real service a way you already trust?
steps.mistake: Trusting a page because it looks official, has a padlock, or avoids scary words.
steps.good: Stop before anything that costs something. Work out what it will do. Then check the service by a route the message did not pick for you.

steps.title: Reading, or allowing?
steps.prompt: Sort each one. Reading or looking hands over nothing. Allowing changes your information, your accounts, your device, your money, or what gets sent in your name.

items.text: Open the Help page inside an app you reached from your own bookmark.
Let an AI add-on read and change everything on every site you visit.
Upload a school document with classmates' names and teacher comments in it.
Read the price and the renewal terms without starting the trial.
Download and open a 'required AI helper' from a message you did not expect.
Tap 'Continue with Google' when the app also wants your files, contacts and email.
Let AI send the email it just drafted, on its own.
Look in your settings to find where connected apps can be switched off.

steps.reveal: The pause comes before you allow, upload, install, pay, post, or send. Not only when one scary word shows up. Reading a screen is not the same as agreeing to it.

lessons.title: Type It, Say It, or Show It
lessons.coreQuestion: When should I type, talk, or show a photo — and how do I give away as little as possible?
lessons.blurb: Three ways into one task. Pick the one that shows least, expect mistakes, and never need a camera to finish.

steps.title: Three ways into one task
steps.scenario:
You want help turning your gran's handwritten recipe into something you can actually read.

You could type the words out. You could read them aloud. You could take a photo, cropped tight on the card.

All three might work. Each one hands over something different. Each one can go wrong in a different way.
steps.prompt: Which would you pick, and what would you check before sending it? There is no single right door. Explain the trade-off.

steps.title: Typing, talking, and showing
steps.body:
Many AI apps take typing, speech, photos, or files. Behind the screen, different parts handle each one.

One part turns sound into words. One part pulls the writing out of a photo. One part looks at a picture and describes what it seems to show. Then the AI writes a reply from that. People call an app that takes several ways in multimodal. It only means more than one door.

The app does not hear or see the way you do. Every one of those steps can slip. Speech gets accents and names wrong. Writing pulled out of a photo mixes up letters and numbers. A picture reader can miss something just outside the crop, or confidently misread a blurry object.

So pick the door that gives the task enough and shows the least. Then compare what it read with what was really there.

Letting an app use your camera or microphone is a permission: you allowing it, and you can take it back. It is never required. You can finish this lesson using the examples here.
steps.mistake: Assuming a photo or your voice is automatically more accurate, or handing over the camera and microphone because it is quicker.
steps.good: Pick a door, keep it narrow, check what it read, and use typing when a camera is not available or not wanted.

steps.title: Which door shows the least?
steps.prompt: Pick the simplest way that still works. Typing is enough whenever you can describe the task in words.

items.text: Ask for three dinner ideas using eggs and rice. You can type two words.
Catch a reminder while your hands are covered in flour, after checking the microphone.
Copy out one handwritten recipe card, cropped so the family name on the back is out of shot.
Rewrite this line: 'Meeting moved two thurday at tree.'
Describe the buttons on a machine you do not know, cropped close, with none of the room in shot.
Think up a title for a project, with no file, photo, or recording at all.

steps.reveal: More doors does not mean send more. Typing usually shows the least. Talking saves effort. A tight crop keeps detail that is slow to type. The best door gives the app only what the task needs.

steps.title: If you want to try it on your own device
steps.body:
If you do test speech or photos in an outside app, use a harmless sentence or a made-up object.

Look at whether it wants access once or forever. Send only what the task needs. Read what it heard or saw before you go on.

On a school device, follow the school's rules. On a shared device, remember the next person.

Skipping this leaves nothing unfinished. The sorting, the ordering, and the misread-word check above are what count.
steps.mistake: Thinking the lesson needs a certain phone, account, camera, microphone, or app.
steps.good: Pick the door that suits your body, your device, your privacy, and the task. Then check what it read.

lessons.title: Your First Real Question
lessons.coreQuestion: What should I bring to AI first: a clever test, or one small real thing from my own week?
lessons.blurb: Hand AI one small real job from your own week. Then actually use the answer and finish it.

steps.title: The thing you keep putting off
steps.scenario:
There is a small thing sitting on your list. A message you owe someone. A shopping list for the week. A reply you keep not writing. A homework question you have been stuck on since Tuesday.

Nothing dramatic. Just a little thing you keep meaning to do and have not.
steps.prompt: Before you read on: what is ONE small real thing from this week you have been meaning to do? Not a made-up test. A real one. Hold it in your head.

steps.title: Real job, or quiz question?
steps.prompt: AI helps you first on small, real, everyday jobs. Not clever demos or trick questions. Sort each one.
buckets: A real job from my week

items.text: Message my coach to say I will miss Thursday training
What year did the French Revolution start?
Make a shopping list for two quick weeknight dinners
Prove that the square root of 2 is irrational
Write a polite message asking my teacher for one more day on an essay

steps.reveal: The real ones are where AI helps you first. Plenty of people think it is only for clever demos or school answers. The opposite is true. Your ordinary little jobs are where it earns its keep.

steps.title: It guesses. It does not know you.
steps.body:
When you describe your situation, the AI is not reading your mind. Here is what really happens. It learned patterns from an enormous amount of human writing. So it guesses the words that usually help someone in a spot like the one you typed.

The more real, ordinary detail you give, the closer that guess lands on YOUR life.

Some apps can also search the web and keep bits of your earlier chats. They still guess. A smooth answer can still be wrong.

Keep the details ordinary. No passwords, no account numbers, nothing private about money or health.

And here is one line worth drawing now. 'Do my homework for me' hands over the exact part that was meant to teach you something. 'I am stuck on question 4, walk me through it' keeps the learning and still gets you moving. Same app. Completely different result for you.
steps.mistake: Typing a vague test ('write a good message') and expecting it to know who it is for.
steps.good: Handing it a real job with a detail or two ('message my coach — I am friendly with him, so warm but short').

steps.prompt: I need help with one small real job: [the actual thing, in your own words]. My situation: [a detail or two — who it is for, how I want to sound, what I already have]. Please [write it / list it / explain it / give me 3 short options], short and in plain language. If you need one thing from me to do it well, ask me first.

My situation: I am friendly with him, so warm but short, and I want to offer to make it up. Please give me 2 short versions I can choose from, in plain language. If you need one thing from me to do it well, ask me first.' If your real job is homework, ask it to walk you through the part you are stuck on, not to hand you the finished answer. Fill the blanks with true details, nothing private about money or health, then read the answer and fix what is off.

lessons.title: How to Ask So It Actually Helps
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I turn a vague ask into one that gets a genuinely useful answer?
lessons.blurb: An ask is an instruction, not a wish. Add four things and watch the answer sharpen.

steps.title: The lazy one-liner
steps.scenario:
You open an AI app and type the first thing in your head: 'give me a study plan.'

It answers instantly. Seven days, no subject, nobody in particular.

It is fine. It is also useless to you.
steps.prompt: Before you read on: the AI did not fail. Given only 'give me a study plan', what did it have to work with? What could you have told it?

steps.title: An ask is an instruction, not a wish
steps.body:
Remember how it works. The AI guesses the words that fit next, from patterns in a huge amount of human writing.

What you type is called a prompt. It just means the words you give it to work from.

So the more you say about what you want, the fewer answers fit, and the closer it lands on you.

The fix is not a longer sentence. A long vague ask still gets a vague answer. Being specific is what helps, not being wordy.

Extra words earn their place only when they tell it something real. That means your goal, who you are, your limits, and the shape you want back.
steps.mistake: Padding a vague ask with more words: 'Please kindly provide a comprehensive and detailed study plan.' Still vague, just longer.
steps.good: Telling it something real: what you want to do, who you are, your limits, and how the answer should look.

steps.title: Which part is missing?
steps.prompt: Each line adds ONE real thing. Is it your Goal and Context — what you want to do, and who you are? Or your Constraints and Format — your limits, and the shape you want back?
buckets: What I want, and who I am
My limits, and the shape I want back

items.text: 'Help me make a 5-day plan for my biology test.'
'I am 15, the test is Friday, and cell diagrams confuse me.'
'I get 45 minutes a night and no weekends.'
'Give it to me as a short table, one row per day.'
'Put one practice question in each day.'

steps.reveal: Goal is what you want to DO. Not 'tell me about X' but 'help me do Y'. Context is who you are, so the answer fits you and not a stranger. Constraints are your limits and must-haves: time, money, reading level, things to leave out. Format is the shape you want back: a list, a table, three sentences, steps.

steps.title: Watch the gap open up
steps.weak: 'give me a study plan' -> a bland week-long plan, no subject, nobody in particular.
steps.strong: 'Goal: help me make a 5-day plan for my biology test. Context: I am 15, the test is Friday, cell diagrams confuse me. Constraints: 45 minutes a night, no weekends, one practice question a day. Format: a short table, one row per day.' -> a plan built around cell diagrams, cut to 45 minutes, with a question every day.
steps.why: Same AI. The strong one just narrowed what could fit. Every part you added threw away a cloud of answers meant for somebody else.

steps.title: Repair a vague ask without oversharing
steps.weak: Make this better. Here is the whole private chat and everyone's names.
steps.strong: Help me [what I want to do]. The background you need is [the background it needs]. Stick to these limits: [my limits]. Give it back as [the shape I want back]. Do not invent facts you do not have. Ask me one question if you need to.

steps.title: If you test it outside, send only what the job needs
steps.body:
If you take your repaired ask into an outside app, those words leave LearningAI. Swap real names, your school, account details, health information, exact addresses, and private messages for made-up stand-ins.

The repair above is what counts. Going outside is optional.

One more thing, about homework. Asking it to write your essay hands over the part that was supposed to teach you. Asking it to explain the step you are stuck on does not. You decide which of those you are asking for, and your Goal is where you say it.
steps.mistake: Adding sensitive detail because more background sounds automatically better.
steps.good: Add background that matters. Do not add yourself.

steps.title: Rebuild your own, one part at a time
steps.prompt: Goal: [what you want to do]. Context: [who you are and your situation]. Constraints: [your limits and must-haves]. Format: [the shape you want back]. Write the answer, then tell me in one line which part of my ask shaped it most.
steps.note: Add the parts one at a time and run it again after each. Goal, run. Add Context, run. Add Constraints, run. Add Format, run. Running again is cheap, because the chat still holds everything you said. Put your first answer and your last one side by side. That gap is the whole lesson. Only share background that matters, and no private details you do not need to hand over.

steps.title: Save your four-part frame

fields.label: Goal — what I want to do
fields.placeholder: help me make a 5-day plan for my biology test

fields.label: Context — who I am
fields.placeholder: I am 15, the test is Friday, cell diagrams confuse me

fields.label: Constraints — my limits
fields.placeholder: 45 min a night, no weekends, one question a day

fields.label: Format — the shape I want back
fields.placeholder: a short table, one row per day: topic, what to do, question

steps.title: You have got it when...
steps.question: Take a fresh weak ask you have not touched today: 'help me plan a birthday party', or 'write a message to my form tutor'. Add the four parts one at a time, running it again each time. What shows you actually get it?

options.text: You can point at the single part that made the biggest difference for THAT ask, and say why.
options.feedback: Yes. The win is not memorising four words. It is knowing what each one is for, and seeing which did the heavy lifting here.

options.text: You wrote the longest, most detailed ask you could.
options.feedback: Length is not the point. A long vague ask still gets a vague answer. Specific beats wordy every time.

options.text: You got a good answer first try without changing anything.
options.feedback: Maybe you got lucky. The skill is steering. If you cannot name what shaped the answer, you cannot repeat it.

options.text: You used the four words Goal, Context, Constraints, Format as headings.
options.feedback: The labels are only scaffolding. What matters is that you put something real under each one.

lessons.title: Fix It With One Reply
lessons.coreQuestion: When an answer is almost right, how do I fix it with one short reply instead of starting again?
lessons.blurb: Nudge a nearly-right answer with one line. No deleting, no retyping.

steps.title: The answer that is almost right
steps.scenario:
You asked for a thank-you message for your aunt. What came back is six stiff sentences. Too long, too formal, nothing like how you talk.

It is close. It is just not quite it.
steps.prompt: Before you read on, what is your first instinct? Delete it and write a better question? Or reply and fix the one you have?

steps.title: The second message is the steering wheel
steps.body:
Here is what is really going on. Inside one chat, the AI can see everything said so far. Your question, its answer, and now your reply.

So a short line like 'shorter, please' arrives as 'redo that last thing, but shorter'.

People say the AI remembers. That is a comparison, not the truth. Your earlier messages are simply still sitting in front of it while it guesses the next ones.

Start a brand-new chat and it can see none of that. You would have to build the whole request again from scratch.

That is why one line is enough to steer.
steps.mistake: Scrapping a close answer and retyping the whole question, throwing away the part that already worked.
steps.good: Sending ONE reply that keeps the good parts and changes only what is off.

steps.title: Retype it, or nudge it
steps.weak: Delete the answer, then retype everything: 'Write me a warm, friendly thank-you message, four sentences, mentioning the dinner, not too formal, that sounds like me...'
steps.strong: Just reply: 'That is close, but it is too long and too formal. Keep the rest the same. Cut it to four sentences and make it friendlier.'
steps.why: The nudge is a fraction of the typing and it keeps everything you already liked. The AI can still see its own answer, so 'keep the rest the same' has something real to hold onto.

steps.title: One change at a time
steps.prompt: You want to steer an answer without losing what worked. Sort each reply by whether it changes ONE clear thing or piles on several.

items.text: Make it shorter — about four sentences.
Make it warmer.
Make it shorter, warmer, add a joke, and change the ending.
Drop the last paragraph.
Rewrite the whole thing completely differently.

steps.reveal: Change ONE thing per reply. Then you can see exactly what each nudge did. If you do not like the result, you know which reply to undo. Five changes at once hide which one mattered.

steps.title: Change one thing and keep the result visible
steps.goal: Improve a message without losing your voice or changing five things at once.
correct: Name the one part that is not working
Protect the parts that already fit
Ask for one change you could point at
Compare the new version with what you actually wanted
Rewrite it and approve the final message yourself
choices: Protect the parts that already fit
Rewrite it and approve the final message yourself
Name the one part that is not working
Compare the new version with what you actually wanted
Ask for one change you could point at
steps.note: If you test a follow-up outside LearningAI, use a made-up draft, or take out names, private messages, and account details first.

steps.title: Send one nudge
steps.prompt: That is close, but [what is off about it]. Keep the rest the same and just [the one change you want].
steps.note: Fill the blanks with the single biggest problem and the exact fix. Example: 'That is close, but it is too long and too formal. Keep the rest the same and just cut it to four sentences and make it friendlier.' Watch it adjust the same answer in place. Still off? Nudge again — 'now add a line about the dinner' — without ever retyping the original question. This works on homework help too: 'that explanation lost me at step 3, explain just that step with an example'.

steps.title: Save your three go-to nudges

fields.label: My length nudge
fields.placeholder: shorter — about four sentences

fields.label: My tone nudge
fields.placeholder: warmer, or less like a textbook

fields.label: My trim nudge
fields.placeholder: drop the last part, keep the rest the same

steps.title: Did you steer it with replies alone?
steps.question: Take a fresh answer you did not like. A new question, not the thank-you message. Improve it using replies only, with nothing retyped. When it comes good, which is true?

options.text: I fixed it with replies alone, and I can name the one nudge that did the work.
options.feedback: That is the skill. You steered the answer you already had, and you know which nudge mattered.

options.text: I deleted it and wrote a stronger question from scratch.
options.feedback: That is starting over. It works, but it throws away the good parts, and it is not the skill here. Try again with replies only.

options.text: I sent one reply changing five things, and I cannot tell which one fixed it.
options.feedback: Change one thing per reply. Otherwise you cannot see which nudge worked, or undo the one that did not.

lessons.title: The One Privacy Rule
lessons.coreQuestion: What is the one question to ask before you send, and what should you take out first?
lessons.blurb: Before you send, ask: would I be fine if this were public? Then scrub whatever you would not.

steps.title: A postcard, not a diary
steps.scenario:
You want help sorting out a charge nobody in your family recognises. You start typing the full card number, the name of the shop worker, and your home address.

It feels private. Just you and a chat box.

But those details leave LearningAI and land in another company's system. And the writing job did not need a single one of them.
steps.prompt: Before you read on: which parts of that message would you not want a stranger to read? Name them.

steps.title: Safe, or never share?
steps.prompt: Sort each one. Safe to type into an AI, or on the never-share list? Never-share means passwords and logins, full ID or bank or account numbers, or another person's full name plus their private business.

items.text: 'There is a charge for about $300 that nobody recognises.'
'Help me write a polite email to the bank.'
My password (even though the message said it was urgent)
'My neighbour Dan Reyes, 14 Oak St, is behind on his medical bills.'
'Someone in my family is having a hard time and I want to help.'

steps.reveal: The rough amount and the request are enough on their own. The account number, the password, the address, and another person's details were never needed. No urgent-sounding message changes that.

steps.title: The one public test
steps.body:
The mistake: 'It is a private chat box, so what I type stays between me and the AI.'

Not quite. What you type goes to the company running it. What happens after that depends on the app, your account, your settings, and their current rules. It might be kept for a while. People there may be allowed to read some of it. It may be used to improve the system. It may come back later through a memory feature. None of those is true of every app, so check the settings and the rules of the one you actually use.

One rule survives all of that. Before you send, ask: would I be fine if this turned up somewhere public? Then take out anything you would not.

Some details do more damage than they look. Your home address and school name together tell a stranger where to find you most days. Swap both for something general.

An AI is a tool. It is not a friend, a counsellor, or someone who can be responsible for you. For anything serious, bring in a real person or a professional you trust.
steps.mistake: Pasting your real message with the card number, the password, and a neighbour's address still in it. All because the box feels private.
steps.good: You decide what leaves your device. Run the public test, then take out every password, full number, and other person's private detail before you send.

steps.title: Blur it before you send
steps.weak: Help me write a polite email about a wrong charge of $312 on [full card number] to [a real person's name], who lives at [home address].
steps.strong: Help me write a polite email about a wrong charge on [my card] for [the amount] to [the shop].

steps.title: Run the privacy scan yourself
steps.goal: Turn a made-up message into one that is safe to send, without relying on another AI to spot the risk.
correct: Circle every real name, exact place, school, workplace, account detail, password, private message, photo, and fact about another person
Delete anything the job does not need
Swap what is left for stand-ins like [a relative], [the amount], or [my card]
Read it back as if it were public, and ask what a stranger could work out
If it could still cause harm or embarrassment, do not send it. Ask a trusted person or a professional instead
steps.note: This scan on its own finishes the activity. No outside app is needed, and none of them should ever be your final judge of what is private.

steps.title: Save your public test

fields.label: What I take out before sending
fields.placeholder: Names, passwords, places, full numbers, private messages

fields.label: Stand-ins I can use instead
fields.placeholder: [a relative], [the amount], [my card]

steps.title: Scrub a brand-new message
steps.question: Take a different message you have not scrubbed yet. Which final version means you have the skill?

options.text: One a stranger could read and learn nothing they could use against me or anyone else. Every private part named, sorted, and swapped for a stand-in.
options.feedback: Exactly. Name each private part, know which kind it is, blur it, and check that a stranger would learn nothing usable.

options.text: One where I left the real details in, because the chat feels private and it is faster.
options.feedback: It only feels private. Your words leave your device, and what happens next depends on the app and its settings. Scrub first.

options.text: One where I took out my own card number but kept a neighbour's full name and home address.
options.feedback: Other people's details count too. A full name plus their address, health, money, or secrets is not yours to hand over.

lessons.title: Who Is in Charge
lessons.coreQuestion: If the AI writes it, who is actually in charge, and which part is still my job?
lessons.blurb: AI can do the middle of a job. You keep the goal, the way you want it, and the last look.

steps.title: It wrote the whole thing. So who decided?
steps.scenario:
Your gran sent you money for your birthday. You ask an AI app to write the thank-you message.

Five seconds later it is there. Neat, polite, finished. You nearly send it.

Then you read the first line. 'Dear valued family member.' You have never said that in your life.
steps.prompt: The AI typed every word. Does that mean it was in charge? Which part of that job was never its to decide?

steps.title: It does the middle. You hold both ends.
steps.body:
The AI wrote every word and still decided nothing. Here is what it actually does.

It has read an enormous amount of human writing. When you type something, it guesses which words usually come next. Then the next. Then the next. That is the whole trick.

Some apps can also search the web, or keep bits of your older chats. They are still guessing.

So it can fill in the middle of a job. It cannot want anything. It has no idea what counts as good to you.

Three jobs stay yours.

The goal. What you actually want.

The way. How you want it done.

The last look. You reading it and saying yes before you use it.

Letting it type for you is not the same as letting it decide for you.
steps.mistake: Handing over the whole thing — 'write my thank-you message' — and sending back whatever turns up.
steps.good: Handing over only the middle. You say the goal and the way. It drafts. You check it before it goes anywhere.

steps.title: Whose job is it?
steps.prompt: Sort each piece of the job. AI can handle the busy middle. Three things stay with you.

items.text: Deciding it should sound warm and like me, not stiff
Writing a first draft in five seconds
Choosing that it stays under four sentences and mentions the money
Looking up a nicer way to word one awkward line
Reading it against what I wanted and saying yes before I send it

steps.reveal: The drafting and the looking-up are the middle. AI is happy to do those. The goal (warm, like me), the way (short, mention the money), and the last look never left you. Those are the two ends you hold.

steps.title: Mark where the job changes hands
steps.goal: Use AI to help make a poster for the school charity match, without letting it make the calls that matter.
correct: You decide who the poster is for and what it has to do
You take out phone numbers and anything private a poster does not need
AI writes a few different layouts to choose from
You check the date, the rules, and how people get in
You pick one, fix what is off, and say yes before it goes up
choices: You check the date, the rules, and how people get in
AI writes a few different layouts to choose from
You pick one, fix what is off, and say yes before it goes up
You take out phone numbers and anything private a poster does not need
You decide who the poster is for and what it has to do
steps.note: If an outside app writes the draft, your words leave LearningAI. Stick to facts a poster on a wall would show anyway. Do not paste lists of names, phone numbers, or private messages.

steps.title: Run one real job and keep the three parts
steps.prompt:
Pick one small real thing you have to do today. Write three lines first: 'My goal is ___.' 'The way I want it is ___.' 'I will check it by ___.' THEN send this:

"Help me with the middle of this. Do not decide it for me: [the job]. My goal is [goal]. I want it done this way: [the way]. Give me a draft I can read, then list 2 or 3 things I should double-check before I trust it."
steps.note: Example fill-ins — job: 'write a short thank-you message to my gran for the birthday money.' goal: 'it sounds warm and like me, not stiff.' way: 'under four sentences, and mention what I am saving up for.' When the draft lands, read it out loud against your goal. Ask: is this what I actually wanted? The moment you feel like just sending it is the moment your check matters most. If the job is homework, ask it to walk you through the bit you are stuck on. Asking it to hand you the finished answer gives away the part that was meant to teach you.

steps.title: Save your three-jobs card

fields.label: My goal
fields.placeholder: What done well means to me, in my own words

fields.label: The way I want it
fields.placeholder: How it should be done — under four sentences, mention the money

fields.label: I will check it by
fields.placeholder: How I test it before I trust it — read it against my goal, check each fact

steps.title: Show that you held the wheel
steps.question: Take a brand-new job of your own, not the thank-you message. Say all three lines before you type anything. Run it, then do your check. What proves you were in charge?

options.text: I can point at the spot where I caught something. A place the draft missed my goal or my way, and I changed it.
options.feedback: Yes. That caught-it moment is the proof. You held the goal, the way, and the last look, and let AI do only the middle.

options.text: The draft was so good I sent it without changing anything.
options.feedback: Sending it untouched means you skipped your check. It can sound sure of itself and still be wrong, or just not what you wanted.

options.text: I handed over the whole job and let the AI work out what good meant.
options.feedback: That gives away the goal, which is the one thing it must not decide. It has no idea what good means to you.

options.text: It finished so fast that there was nothing left to check.
options.feedback: Speed is not a check. Fast and confident is exactly when a made-up detail slips past you. Read it anyway.

lessons.title: Check It Before You Trust It
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I tell whether the source an AI gives me really backs up what it said?
lessons.blurb: A link proves nothing until you open it and find the fact sitting there on the page.

steps.title: The answer that looks airtight
steps.scenario:
You ask an AI app a question for your class presentation. The answer comes back sounding certain.

Underneath it lists where the fact came from. A title, a writer, a date, even a link that opens.

It looks solid. Your slide is nearly done.
steps.prompt: What has the AI actually proved by handing you that link? That the page is real? That the page says the thing it claimed?

steps.title: A source is decoration until you open it
steps.body:
A source is simply where a fact came from. A website, a book, a report by people who study that thing.

Here is the problem. The AI guesses words that fit the shape of a good answer. A tidy source name fits that shape perfectly. So it can hand you one that is out of date, is about something else, or was never real at all.

There is a second trap, and it catches more people. Plenty of apps really do search the web. They give you a genuine link that genuinely opens. That still proves nothing on its own. The page may simply not say what the AI said it says.

The link opening is not the test. The page saying the thing is the test.

Think of a receipt. Anyone can print one. You only believe it once you see the money actually gone from the account. That is a comparison, not the real thing. What is really happening is plainer: the AI wrote something shaped like a good source, and nothing checked it.
steps.mistake: It gave me a link and an author, so the answer must be backed up.
steps.good: I open it myself, see that it is real, and find the fact on the page before I trust it.

steps.title: Three checks, in this order
steps.goal: Turn one AI claim plus its source into a verdict you can defend
correct: Ask the AI for its single best source, and the exact sentence in it that backs the answer
Open it yourself — click the link, or search the title and the writer's name
Check 1 — Is it there? Does the link open, or does the title turn up at all?
Check 2 — Is it a real place: a known site, a proper study, a real organisation?
Check 3 — Does it actually say it? Can you find that exact fact on the page?
Give it one word: Checked, Does not match, or Not found
steps.note: A page that wants you to pay or log in is not proof it is fake. 'I cannot open it' is not the same as 'it does not exist.' Try another way in before you judge. If any of the three checks fails, the claim is not proven, and you just caught it in time.

steps.title: Judge a source trail
steps.claim: A local swimming pool lets anyone under 16 swim on their own after 6 p.m.
steps: Write down exactly what is being allowed, and who it affects
Go to the pool's own current rules, not to another AI answer
Check the place, the age rule, the date, and any exceptions
Write down one word: Checked, Does not match, or Not found
If it is still unclear, do not act until the pool or a responsible adult confirms it
steps.note: This trail is enough to practise on. It uses no real names, no real address, and nobody's actual timetable.

steps.title: If you go outside, keep the question clean
steps.body:
If you carry on in an outside app, your words leave LearningAI. Pick a public claim that does not matter much.

Do not share a real person's name, age, timetable, health detail, account number, or private message.

The source you open is what earns the verdict. Not the chatbot.
steps.mistake: Adding personal details to make a public fact easier to look up.
steps.good: Asking about the public claim only, then going and reading the source yourself.

steps.title: Ask for the source AND the exact sentence
steps.prompt: Answer this question: [question]. Then give me the single best source for it, the exact sentence from that source that backs it up, and a link, or the title, writer and date. Keep it to [number] source(s). I am going to open it and check that it really says this, so do not invent anything. If you are not sure a real source exists, say so instead.
steps.note: For [question], pick one specific fact that should have a real, findable source. Something like: how much water should an adult drink in a day, and who says so? For [number], start with one. Use two if you want a second opinion. Then actually open it and run the three checks.

steps.title: Save your check-a-claim card

fields.label: The claim I am checking
fields.placeholder: Adults should drink 8 cups of water a day

fields.label: The source it gave me
fields.placeholder: A link, or a title, writer and date

fields.label: The sentence that should prove it
fields.placeholder: Paste the sentence the AI quoted

fields.label: My verdict after opening it
fields.placeholder: Checked / Does not match / Not found — and the sentence that earns it

steps.title: Earn a verdict on a claim of your own
steps.question: Pick a brand-new question of your own, not the water one. Run the prompt and open the source. What counts as doing this well?

options.text: The AI wrote 'verified', so I am done. Getting that word back is the goal.
options.feedback: The AI's own word is not the check. The win is you reaching a verdict by opening the source, whatever that verdict turns out to be.

options.text: I opened the source and ran the three checks. Then I wrote one word: Checked, Does not match, or Not found. I can point at the exact sentence that earns it, or at the fact it is missing.
options.feedback: That is it. Reaching a verdict you can defend on a fresh claim is the win, not collecting a tick.

options.text: The link opened and the page looked professional, so I trusted the claim without reading it.
options.feedback: That is the modern trap. A working link proves the page exists. Check 3 is the one that matters.

options.text: The page wanted me to pay, so I marked the claim as made up.
options.feedback: A paywall is not proof of anything. 'I cannot open it' is not 'it does not exist.' Try another way in first.

lessons.title: AI Is Already in Your Apps
lessons.coreQuestion: Where is AI quietly shaping what an app shows me, and what should change how much I trust it?
lessons.blurb: Spot the quiet AI bits in apps you already use. Read what the app itself says they do. Check harder when a mistake would cost you.

steps.title: Nothing announced itself
steps.scenario:
Your photo app has quietly gathered every picture of your best friend into one folder. Your email offers you a ready-made reply. A search page writes you a paragraph before any of the links.

None of them said 'this is AI'. Each one is doing a different job, and the same app can behave differently on a school account.
steps.prompt: Before you rely on one of these, which matters more: whether the word AI appears anywhere, or what happens if it gets it wrong?

steps.title: Look at the evidence, not the buzzword
steps.prompt: Sort each clue by what it can honestly tell you. These are all built in, so you do not need any particular phone.
buckets: Tells me something real about this feature

items.text: The app's own help page says photo search matches faces, and shows how to fix a wrong match.
A chatbot says the feature 'probably uses AI somewhere'.
A setting names the feature, shows whether it is on, and says what it is allowed to look at.
The answer arrived fast and looked futuristic.
Your school says this feature is switched off on school accounts.
A friend has the same app and assumes every account works the same.

steps.reveal: A label, a slick animation, or a confident guess tells you nothing about how one feature works. The app's own help page, the settings you can see, and your school's rules are far stronger. Even then, stay on the choice in front of you. What does the feature do? What can it see? What would a mistake cost?

steps.title: Lots of different jobs, not one hidden brain
steps.body:
AI inside everyday apps is not one recipe copied everywhere. Different parts do different jobs.

One puts search results in an order. One matches pictures to each other. One turns speech into text. One writes new sentences or makes new images.

Plenty of features mix a guessing part with plain fixed rules, or with a person checking the result.

You do not have to name every piece before you use something. You need enough to answer four questions.

What job is this feature doing?

What is it allowed to see?

Can I turn it off, correct it, or undo a mistake?

What changes if it gets it wrong?
steps.mistake: Treating 'AI' as one yes-or-no label, then trusting or refusing every feature the same way.
steps.good: Looking at the actual feature and its settings, then checking harder as the cost of a mistake goes up.

steps.title: Look before you lean on it
steps.goal: A calendar app suggests a time for your study group. Get it wrong and somebody turns up to an empty room. Put the check in order.
correct: Name the thing you might rely on: the time it suggested
Read the app's own label, help page, settings, or your school's rules, instead of asking another AI to guess
Check what it looked at, and whether you can correct the suggestion or switch it off
Compare the suggestion with the real calendar entry, because getting it wrong costs somebody an afternoon
If it is wrong, fix the entry, then change or switch off the feature before next time
choices: Compare the suggestion with the real calendar entry, because getting it wrong costs somebody an afternoon
Name the thing you might rely on: the time it suggested
If it is wrong, fix the entry, then change or switch off the feature before next time
Check what it looked at, and whether you can correct the suggestion or switch it off
Read the app's own label, help page, settings, or your school's rules, instead of asking another AI to guess
steps.note: If a mistake costs nothing, this takes seconds. For health, money, school, work, safety, or somebody else's private information, slow down and check a source that actually knows.

steps.title: Optional: look up one real feature
steps.prompt: Pick one ordinary feature you can safely look into. Or use this one: 'an email app offers a ready-made reply.' Find the app's own label, help text, or setting. Write down four things: what job it says it does, what control you have, one way it could be wrong, and how you would fix it if it were.
steps.note: You do not need to list your real apps or devices. Do not share account names, contacts, messages, photos, school details, or where you have been. If the app explains nothing, write 'not stated' rather than asking a chatbot to invent an explanation.

fields.label: The feature and its job
fields.placeholder: Calendar suggests a time for the study group

fields.label: What tells me how it works
fields.placeholder: The help page, a setting, or a school rule

fields.label: What a mistake would cost
fields.placeholder: Somebody turns up to an empty room

fields.label: How I fix it or switch it off
fields.placeholder: Compare with the invite, fix it, then turn suggestions off

steps.title: Pick the check that actually holds up
steps.question: A writing app quietly rewrites a sentence in a message to your teacher. Which response shows the whole skill?

options.text: I find the rewrite setting and read what it says it does. Then I reread the changed sentence, because this message matters, and undo it if the meaning shifted.
options.feedback: Yes. You used what you could actually see, checked harder because it mattered, and kept a way to undo it.

options.text: It looks like AI, so I decide it is unsafe and never open the app again.
options.feedback: The label alone does not settle it. Look at the feature, its settings, and what a mistake would cost.

options.text: I ask a different chatbot whether this app uses AI, and believe whatever it says.
options.feedback: That is one more guess. Use the app's own help page, the settings you can see, and any school rule.

options.text: Grammar changes are usually harmless, so I send it without rereading.
options.feedback: The cost depends on this message, not on the type of feature. A changed meaning going to a teacher is worth ten seconds.

lessons.title: A Daily Habit, Not a Crutch
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I use AI every day so my own thinking gets sharper instead of switching off?
lessons.blurb: Use AI often, without handing over the part you wanted your own brain to learn.

steps.title: Two ways to use the same app
steps.scenario:
Your friend's mum has driven you to football three weekends running. You owe her a thank-you text.

You could type 'write a thank-you text' and send back whatever appears. Or you could write a rough one yourself, then ask AI to tighten it.

Same job. Same app. Same five minutes.
steps.prompt: After each of those, which one leaves something behind in your head? A sentence you shaped, a choice you made. Say it in one line.

steps.title: Crutch, or coach?
steps.prompt: Underneath, the AI is guessing likely next words either way. What changes is what you ask for. Sort each one: does it think for you, or does it make you think and then help?

items.text: "Write my whole essay on this book."
"I will write the reply first. Then show me two lines I could cut."
"Just give me the answer to this maths question."
"Ask me a question that shows whether I actually understood the chapter."
"Rewrite this so it sounds clever. I do not want to touch it."
"Wait for my attempt, then tell me one thing to fix next time."

steps.reveal: Same machine, different instructions. Crutch and coach are a comparison to help you feel the difference. They are not a claim about what is going on inside. These apps can search, take several steps, and sometimes keep bits of old chats. None of that lets them choose which of your own skills you want to protect. You draw that line.

steps.title: A good habit ends with your brain switched on
steps.body:
Using AI every day does not make you lazy on its own. It depends entirely on how you use it.

Here is what it does. It has read an enormous amount of human writing, and it guesses the words that usually come next. Ask it to do the job, and it does the job. Your brain stays off.

Ask it to make you try first and only then help, and it waits. Your brain stays on.

A good habit is one that leaves your thinking sharper afterwards, not switched off.

One more thing. AI is not a friend, and it is not a doctor or a counsellor. For anything about your health, your safety, or a hard personal decision, bring in a real person you trust.
steps.mistake: "Write this for me." You paste the result, learn nothing, and the skill never becomes yours.
steps.good: "I will do my part first, then you help." You keep one step for yourself, so the skill stays yours.

steps.title: Run your coach habit once, now
steps.prompt: This step uses an outside app, so anything you type leaves LearningAI. Use a made-up example. Do not paste names, private messages, school details, or anyone else's information. I want a 5-minute habit that makes me sharper at [an area, for example writing clear messages] instead of dependent on you. Don't do the work for me — make me try first, then coach me. The one step I will always do myself is: [your step]. Give me one small practice task, wait for my try, then point out one thing worth improving.
steps.note: Pick an ordinary practice task: a pretend reply to a customer, a made-up thank-you, a plan for a game, a short explanation of something you learned. Do your attempt before it helps. If it jumps in early, say: 'Stop. Wait for my attempt first.'
