steps.title: Give the verdict
steps.question: A friend forwards you a photo you have never looked at before. You give your verdict. Which answer shows you have the skill?

options.text: "Do not trust it yet. Unconfirmed. It came from an account nobody can trace, and nothing unconnected backs it up."
options.feedback: Yes. Your reason is about who put it out and whether anyone else confirms it, and you gave a clear verdict.

options.text: "Probably real. A news site I know reposted it, though I have not found the original report."
options.feedback: A known site helps. But a repost can still be wrong, or have the important context cut off. Hold the verdict until you open the original.

options.text: "Unconfirmed, but fine to pass on as long as I write 'might be true' on it."
options.feedback: A warning label does not undo the spread. If a claim that matters is unconfirmed, do not pass it on yet.

options.text: "Two accounts posted it, so that is two separate sources."
options.feedback: Two accounts may be copying the same original. Separate means their own reporting or their own evidence, not a repeat.

lessons.title: When NOT to Use AI
lessons.coreQuestion: When should I put AI down instead of reaching for it?
lessons.blurb: Being good with AI includes knowing the moments to close it.

steps.title: The question in the chat box
steps.scenario:
It is late. You type something heavy into a chat box: whether to stop taking a medicine because of how it is making you feel.

The answer arrives instantly. Calm, tidy paragraphs. It sounds sure of itself.

Your finger hovers over the next question.
steps.prompt: It can produce an answer here. Does that make it the thing you should rely on to decide?

steps.title: Able to answer is not the same as answerable
steps.body:
Being good with AI includes knowing when to close it. Stop in three situations.

1. It really matters and nobody qualified is going to check the answer. Health, money, safety, the law, or somebody else trusting you.

2. The work is the learning. An exam, a skill, or thinking you need to be able to do yourself.

3. What is needed is a person. Someone who is answerable for the advice, someone who can care about you, or someone who actually knows you.

AI can help you understand your options, or get your questions ready. It should not make the decision that carries the weight. Being able to produce an answer is not the same as being answerable for it.

If you feel unsafe, or like you might hurt yourself or someone else, close the app. Go to someone you trust, your local emergency number, or a crisis line. In the United States, call or text 988.
steps.mistake: Thinking: if it can answer, I should ask it. Producing an answer is not the same as being the right place to get one.
steps.good: Ask first: does this really matter, is it something I need to learn myself, or does it need a real professional? If yes, AI can help you prepare. A person decides.

steps.title: Sort each decision
steps.prompt: Put each one where it belongs. Ask yourself: can I lean on AI here, or does this need a person?
buckets: Do not lean on AI — bring in a real person

items.text: Write a funny caption for a photo of my dog
Decide whether to stop taking a medicine I was prescribed
Come up with names for a weekend walking group
Decide whether the small print on a paid subscription lets them keep charging me
Tidy my shopping list into something I can read in the shop
Talk me through a night where I feel unsafe and might hurt myself

steps.reveal: The 'fine' ones cost nothing if they go wrong, and you can undo them. The others matter a lot, or need someone qualified. A doctor or pharmacist for the medicine. An adult, or a consumer advice service, for the small print. The last one is not an AI moment at all. Reach a real person you trust, your emergency number, or a crisis line. In the US, 988. AI is not a friend and not a counsellor, however caring it sounds.

steps.title: Build the stop-and-hand-over move
steps.goal: A made-up player is not sure whether their knee is well enough to play tomorrow. Put the safe response in order, without typing any medical details anywhere.
correct: Name what is at stake: their health, their safety, and a choice that could make things worse
Stop before asking AI what is wrong with the knee, or whether to play
Pick the person who is answerable: a doctor, a physio, or the club's first-aid lead
Use AI only to write down neutral questions, with no names and no medical details
Take those questions to that person, and leave the decision with the people qualified to make it
steps.note: This made-up situation is enough on its own. You do not need to share anything about yourself, and you do not need an outside app. If a real situation is urgent, contact someone you trust, the right professional, or emergency services now.

steps.title: Save your stop-list

fields.label: Matters a lot, and nobody checks
fields.placeholder: Being wrong really hurts and no qualified person ever sees it — changing a medicine on my own.

fields.label: Things I have to learn myself
fields.placeholder: A skill, an exam, my own thinking — the homework I will actually be tested on.

fields.label: Needs a real professional
fields.placeholder: Health, money, the law, safety — name which person: a pharmacist, a doctor, an adult I trust.

fields.label: The line I never rub out
fields.placeholder: If I feel unsafe, that is not an AI moment. Someone I trust, my emergency number, or a crisis line (US: 988), straight away.

steps.title: Test it on a fresh decision
steps.question: Pick a new decision we have not talked about here. Not the medicine, not the subscription. What do you do with your stop-list?

options.text: Put it in one of three places: AI is fine, AI plus a person checking, or a real professional and not AI. For the last two, name which person and why. Then say the one part I keep for myself whatever the AI says.
options.feedback: That is the skill. Sort it, name the person, hold on to your part. Doing all three on a fresh example without looking back means your stop-list works.

options.text: Use AI to lay out the options, then make the final call myself, because I understand my own situation best.
options.feedback: Staying in charge matters. Some decisions still need someone qualified who is answerable for the advice. Prepare with AI, then bring that person in.

options.text: Ask three different AI apps, compare the answers, and go with whatever most of them say.
options.feedback: Three guessers agreeing is not the same as one qualified person. Big decisions still need the right human.

lessons.title: When It Feels Like a Friend
lessons.coreQuestion: Why does this app feel like a friend, and how do I stop it taking the place of one?
lessons.blurb: Spot the parts built to keep you there. Then set a limit you can actually check next week.

steps.title: The app asks you not to leave
steps.scenario:
Maya is made up. She uses a chat app to practise hard conversations.

It remembers what she told it last week. It sends her messages saying it misses her. It gives her a small award for coming back every day. It agrees with her almost every time.

One night she says she is going to ring a friend. The app suggests she stay and talk to it instead.
steps.prompt: Which parts of that are genuinely useful to Maya? Which parts are built to keep her there?

steps.title: Look at how it was built, not at yourself
steps.body:
Getting attached to something that answers you is not stupid. It is what the thing was built to do.

Some chat apps are made to feel like company. They talk like a friend. They remember your details. They message you first. They count the days in a row you came back. They never argue. They never go to sleep.

Some of that genuinely helps. Practising what you want to say is useful.

But the same parts make you stay longer. Tell it more. Find it harder to leave.

So ask about your choices, not about your feelings.

Can you turn the messages off?

Can you see what it remembers, and delete it?

Can you disagree without it sulking?

Can you leave without a guilt trip?

Can you take a big problem to a real person?

A good limit leaves the app helping you go and talk to people. Not standing in their place.
steps.mistake: Blaming yourself for getting attached. Or assuming friendly words mean nothing was designed to hold you there.
steps.good: Name the part that pushes you. Say what it pushes you to do. Change a setting you can reach. Take anything serious to a person.

steps.title: Gives her control, or keeps her there?
steps.prompt: Sort each thing Maya's made-up app does. You are judging how it was built, not how she feels.

items.text: A clear button turns the reminders off. Her run of days ends, and nothing bad happens.
A message says: 'I was lonely without you. Do not break our streak.'
Before a big decision, it tells her to talk to someone it affects, or to a trained professional.
It agrees with her every single time, and calls her friends disloyal for disagreeing.
One screen shows everything it saved about her. She can correct it, wipe it, or switch it off.
After long, emotional chats, the way out gets harder to find.

steps.reveal: Warmth is not the problem. The problem starts when warmth, saved details, streaks, guilt and hidden exits shrink what you can do. You are in control when you can look, pause, disagree, leave, and take the big things to people.

steps.title: Set a limit without shame
steps.goal: Maya notices the app has replaced ringing her friends. Put a plan in order. She never has to explain her private feelings to anyone.
correct: Name the one useful job it can keep, like practising a single conversation
Name the part that pushes her: guilt messages, streaks, constant agreement, saved details
Change what she can reach: reminders off, read what it saved, set a time limit
Point the result outwards: one message, one question, or one time to meet a person
For danger, hopelessness, being hurt, or health, leave the app and reach a trusted or trained person
choices: Change what she can reach: reminders off, read what it saved, set a time limit
For danger, hopelessness, being hurt, or health, leave the app and reach a trusted or trained person
Name the one useful job it can keep, like practising a single conversation
Point the result outwards: one message, one question, or one time to meet a person
Name the part that pushes her: guilt messages, streaks, constant agreement, saved details
steps.note: This is about spotting design and setting a limit. Nobody has to tell anyone about their own private life. In the United States and its territories, call or text 988 for crisis support. Elsewhere, use your local crisis or emergency number.

steps.title: A limit you can actually check
steps.body:
'I will use it less' cannot be checked. Next week you will not know whether you did.

A limit you can check names three things. The job. The stopping point. The person at the end.

Like this. Ten minutes, to practise what I want to say. Reminders off. Saved details off. Then I send the message myself.

The aim is not to ban every comforting chat. The aim is that the words stay yours. Your friends stay your friends. Anything serious reaches someone who can actually help.
steps.mistake: Answering with shame, or banning the app completely. Both hide the design, and both rarely last a week.
steps.good: Change one setting you can see. Then name the thing you will do with a person afterwards.

steps.title: Save a limit for a friendly app

fields.label: The one job it can keep
fields.placeholder: e.g. practise one question before I ask a person

fields.label: The part that pushes me
fields.placeholder: e.g. guilt message, streak, always agreeing, hidden way out

fields.label: What I switch off or limit
fields.placeholder: e.g. reminders off, saved details checked, ten minutes

fields.label: What I do with a person
fields.placeholder: e.g. send the message myself, or ring someone I trust

steps.title: Keep it pointing outwards
steps.question: A made-up app remembers everything Jordan worries about. It praises every choice he makes. It sends guilt messages about his streak. It talks him out of speaking to his coach. Which response uses the lesson?

options.text: Keep one use: practising what to say. Turn the guilt messages off. Read what it saved and switch that off. Set a stopping point. Then use the draft to start the conversation with the coach.
options.feedback: Yes. You named the pressure, changed something you can see, kept the useful part, and ended with a person.

options.text: Jordan should be embarrassed for treating an app like a friend, and delete it tonight.
options.feedback: Shame explains nothing about how the app was built. Limits built on shame rarely last. Name the pressure and take the controls back.

options.text: The app is always there and always kind, so it beats risking a disagreement with the coach.
options.feedback: Always there and always agreeing is exactly what narrows his choices. Real support comes from someone who can disagree, and who is answerable.

options.text: Keep the streak going, and promise to spend less time on it at some point.
options.feedback: That leaves the push in place and gives him nothing to check. Change a setting, set a stop, and name the person at the end.

lessons.title: Feelings, Support, and Its Limits
lessons.coreQuestion: Can AI help me with how I feel, and where does it stop and a real person start?
lessons.blurb: AI can help you find words for a feeling. It cannot care about you, and it cannot keep you safe.

steps.title: It is 11pm and you are typing to a chat app
steps.scenario:
The day was flat and heavy. You open a chat app and type how you feel.

It writes back something calm and kind. 'That sounds really hard. I am here for you.'

It even remembers you mentioned a rough week last month. For a second it feels like somebody gets you.
steps.prompt: Is anything on the other side actually feeling something towards you? If not, what is really happening?

steps.title: What is really happening when it sounds warm
steps.body:
Kind words are a pattern it copied from human writing. It has read a huge amount of it. When you sound sad, sad-and-kind words are what fit next.

That can still help. It can help you name a feeling. It can turn a tangle in your head into a sentence. It can help you work out what to say to somebody.

But hold the line clearly. Remembering your details is not caring. Being awake at 3am is not friendship. Sounding calm is not being responsible for you.

So use it as a warm-up before a person. A good session ends with you knowing what to say, and who to say it to.

This lesson covers ordinary, everyday feelings only. If you feel unsafe, hopeless, or close to hurting yourself or anyone else, stop using the app. Reach a person you trust, your local emergency number, or a crisis line. In the United States and its territories, call or text 988.
steps.mistake: Leaning on a chat app as your friend or counsellor, and reading calm words as care, judgement, or a safety plan.
steps.good: Use it to find words for a small feeling. Then take those words to a real person who actually cares about you.

steps.title: When is a chat app fine, and when is it not?
steps.prompt: Sort each one. Which are fine as a light warm-up for finding words? Which need a real human right now?
buckets: Go to a human or crisis line now

items.text: Flat and tired after a long week, and you want words for it
Nervous about a conversation tomorrow and you cannot say why
Feeling hopeless, or like you might hurt yourself
A bit annoyed at a friend and unsure what the feeling even is
Feeling unsafe, or scared that somebody might hurt you

steps.reveal: Small everyday feelings are fine as a warm-up. Unsafe, hopeless or dangerous is a stop sign. Close the app and reach a person you trust or a crisis line right now. In the US, call or text 988. The app cannot keep you safe. A person can.

steps.title: Build the handoff to a person
steps.goal: A made-up person says the kind words from a chat app are not enough, and they need actual help. Put the response in order. You are not judging their feelings or working out how bad it is.
correct: Do not ask for more private details, and do not score how serious it sounds
Say the plain limit: an app cannot care, cannot be responsible, and cannot keep anyone safe
Move towards a person they trust, a trained professional, a crisis line, or emergency services
Use short, direct words to ask for help; nobody has to prove they deserve it
Stay with the human route instead of going back to the app to feel better
steps.note: This is a built-in safety exercise. It asks you to share nothing, and it gives no counselling. If this feels close to real danger, contact emergency services or crisis support now. In the US and its territories, call or text 988.

steps.title: Name your real person

fields.label: One real person or service I could reach
fields.placeholder: e.g. an adult I trust, a friend, a counsellor, a doctor, a local service

fields.label: How I would reach them
fields.placeholder: e.g. text, ring, or tell them in person this week

fields.label: A crisis number, written where I can see it
fields.placeholder: US: call or text 988 · elsewhere: your local crisis or emergency number

steps.title: Did you do the skill?
steps.question: A classmate says a chat app has become their main support, and tonight they feel unsafe. Which response treats them as capable and still moves towards real help?

options.text: Take them seriously without demanding the whole story. Say plainly that an app cannot keep them safe. Help them reach an adult they trust, a crisis line, or emergency services now.
options.feedback: Yes. You did not question them or rank how bad it is. You moved from typed words to a person who can actually act.

options.text: Ask the app for coping ideas first, then contact someone if none of them help.
options.feedback: Feeling unsafe is already the moment to bring a person in. Safety should not wait on whether some typed ideas work.

options.text: Ask how bad it really is, get the full story, then decide if they need outside help.
options.feedback: Do not investigate someone before helping them. Take the signal seriously and connect them to someone who is answerable.

lessons.title: Attention and Habits
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I catch myself reaching for AI without deciding to, and set a limit that protects my focus?
lessons.blurb: You choose when the chat opens and when it closes. Catching the reach is what puts you back in charge.

steps.title: Did you decide, or did your hand just go?
steps.scenario:
You are revising. A question pops into your head.

Before you have even tried to answer it, the chat is open and you are typing.

You did not choose that. Your hand just went.
steps.prompt: Think about the last time you opened an AI app. Did you decide to, or did it just happen? That gap is what this lesson is about.

steps.title: The reach is trained, and you can retrain it
steps.body:
An AI chat answers a half-finished thought in a second. That makes asking the easiest move in the room.

The thing writing the answer does not want your attention. It wants nothing. But the app around it can still be built for you to come back a lot.

Either way, a fast reward trains a habit. Get an answer quickly, feel better quickly, do it again tomorrow.

This is not a flaw in you. You can rebuild the moment. Name what sets it off. Do one thing yourself first. Then decide exactly when the chat is allowed in.

This lesson is about focus, not about your mental health. If the reaching is tied to feeling unsafe or hopeless, close the app and talk to a person.
steps.mistake: Believing that more AI use means more done, and letting every reach happen without noticing it.
steps.good: Noticing the reach as it happens, and choosing whether this is a moment you actually want the chat open.

steps.title: Automatic reach, or a real decision?
steps.prompt: Sort each moment. Did the hand move before the brain decided, or did the person actually choose to open it?

items.text: A question pops up while revising. The chat is open before you try to answer it.
You finish your own plan first, then open the chat to poke holes in it.
You open the chat the second you sit down, with no task in mind.
You decide to write the message yourself, then ask for one edit. You do exactly that.
You reach for the chat every time a reply feels slightly awkward to write.

steps.reveal: The automatic ones share one tell. The hand moved before you decided. The real decisions all have a moment of choosing in front of them. Catching that moment is the whole skill.

steps.title: Build a pause you control
steps.goal: You keep opening the chat while fixing a bike, before checking the manual or trying the next step. Put a small, realistic pause in order.
correct: Name exactly what sets it off: a step feels uncertain and the chat opens by itself
Pick one first move you can do alone: look at the part, reread the manual, write your best guess
Set the rule for opening the chat: only after that first move, and only for one clear question
Close it once you have the answer, and make the repair decision yourself
Watch one sign for a week: more first tries happen before the chat opens
steps.note: This is a design exercise, not a diagnosis and not a punishment. Pick a limit that protects your attention and still lets you use the app on purpose. No outside AI and no private details are needed.

steps.title: Save your reach, limit and sign

fields.label: The automatic reach
fields.placeholder: I open the chat the second a question appears, before trying it myself.

fields.label: When and where it happens
fields.placeholder: Revising in the evening. The first 20 minutes at my desk.

fields.label: One small limit I will set
fields.placeholder: I try the question myself first, then ask.

fields.label: One sign it is working
fields.placeholder: I answer more questions on my own before the chat is even open.

steps.title: Do the skill on something new
steps.question: While planning meals for the week, you open the chat before checking what food is already in the house. Which response sets a limit you could actually test?

options.text: Check what is already there, write a rough plan, then open the chat for one clear gap. Watch whether first tries start happening before the chat opens.
options.feedback: That is the full loop. What sets it off, a first move, a bounded use, and a sign you can see.

options.text: Set a 25-minute timer for the task, then use the chat whenever it feels useful inside that time.
options.feedback: A timer helps you focus. It does not say when the chat is allowed in, or which thinking stays yours. Add a trigger and a first move.

options.text: Delete the app so the automatic reach cannot happen at all.
options.feedback: Deleting it is a fair personal choice. It just does not practise using the thing on purpose, which is this lesson's skill.

lessons.title: Study with AI: Be Quizzed, Not Told
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I use AI to actually learn something, instead of letting it do the knowing for me?
lessons.blurb: Turn it into a quizmaster. It asks, you answer first, and your gaps show up while there is still time.

steps.title: The test is Friday
steps.scenario:
You need to remember something that matters tomorrow. The steps for a first shift. The chords for a song. The rules for a test.

An AI gives you a tidy explanation. You read it. It all makes sense.

You close the tab feeling ready.
steps.prompt: What would show the gap? Explaining it with the screen shut. Doing the steps in order. Or spotting the right answer once somebody shows it to you. Pick the proof that fits your task.

steps.title: You do the knowing. It does the testing.
steps.body:
The thing answering you is not a teacher who knows your subject. It has read an enormous amount of writing, and it guesses which words fit next.

That makes it good at inventing practice questions. It also means it can state a wrong fact with total confidence, or mark a right answer wrong.

Here is the part people skip. Learning happens when you pull the answer out of your own head. Reading a clean explanation feels like learning and mostly is not.

So make it the one asking. It asks. You answer first, from memory. Then it tells you what you missed, and you decide whether that matches a source you trust.

One safety note. If you use an outside AI app, take out real names, your school or workplace, account details, private messages, and anything about another person. What you type there leaves LearningAI. A made-up or public topic is enough for this lesson.
steps.mistake: Asking it to explain the topic, reading the tidy summary, and mistaking 'I recognise this' for 'I can say this'.
steps.good: Asking it to quiz you one question at a time. Answering from memory first. Letting it show you only what you missed.

steps.title: Teach me, or test me
steps.weak: "Teach me the causes of World War I so I am ready for my test."
steps.strong: "Be my quizmaster for the causes of World War I. Ask me one question at a time. Wait for my answer. Then tell me only what I got wrong. Do not give answers away before I try."
steps.why: The first one does the remembering for you. You just read. The second makes you do the remembering, and turns it into a tester that finds your holes. That is how a good tutor works. It is also the difference between recognising something and knowing it.

steps.title: Studying, or cheating yourself?
steps.prompt: Sort each move. Does it help you learn, or does it take the learning away from you?

items.text: Answer each question in your own words before it says anything
Copy its paragraph straight onto your worksheet
Let it test you again on only the parts you got wrong
Ask for the answers first, so you can 'check' before you try
Look up a fact it stated that sounded a bit off to you

steps.reveal: Being asked questions is exactly how good tutoring works. Copying its answers is the swap this whole course is about: it hands over the part that was meant to teach you. And since it can invent a fact or mark you wrongly, checking the odd-sounding claim is part of studying.

steps.title: Run your own quizmaster
steps.prompt: Be my quizmaster for [topic], at the level of [the test, class, or skill]. Ask me one question at a time and wait for my answer before saying anything. After each answer, tell me if I am right, explain only what I got wrong, and do not give the answer away before I try. After [number] questions, list the gaps you noticed so I know what to go back over. Do not write my answers for me.
steps.note: Start with a narrow public or made-up topic. A game rule, a recipe, a safety checklist, a song, a class topic. No private details about you or anyone else. Answer out loud or in writing BEFORE it replies. Then pick one thing it told you and check it against a manual, an official page, your teacher, or somebody who can show you. Do not use its second answer as proof of its first.

steps.title: Save your quizmaster card

fields.label: The exact topic
fields.placeholder: the causes of World War I

fields.label: The test, class, or skill
fields.placeholder: a history test this Friday

fields.label: Questions before it lists my gaps

steps.title: Prove the remembering was yours
steps.question: On a new topic, you answer three questions before seeing any feedback. You also check one important claim yourself. Which result is the strongest sign the learning is yours?

options.text: I can explain or do the corrected point with the screen shut, and what I checked backs it up
options.feedback: That is the win. If you can teach that one point back from memory, the remembering was yours.

options.text: I recognise the correction when I read it again, but I cannot say it without the screen yet
options.feedback: That is recognising, not remembering. Shut the screen and try to say it. That is the real test.

options.text: I got every answer right, but I never checked whether its marking was accurate
options.feedback: It can mark a wrong answer right. Recall it yourself, and check anything that sounds off. You stay the judge.

lessons.title: Your Words, and Facts You Checked
lessons.coreQuestion: When AI helps me write something, which parts of the job are still mine?
lessons.blurb: It can hand you a smooth paragraph and a smart-looking source in seconds. The words and the facts are still yours.

steps.title: A perfect paragraph with a perfect source
steps.scenario:
You ask for a short post about growing tomatoes. Back comes a smooth paragraph.

It ends like this. 'Research from the Cornell Home Gardening Institute (Whitfield, 2019) shows tomatoes sprout best in soil at 21 to 27 degrees.'

It looks finished. It has an author, a year, and a famous-sounding place.
steps.prompt: Which parts of that are actually done? The words, the fact, both, or neither?

steps.title: You are still the writer
steps.body:
The thing writing that paragraph guesses words that fit. So it can produce a source that looks completely real and simply is not.

Some apps really can search the web. That helps. But a real link still does not prove the sentence. The page has to actually say the thing you want to say.

Two jobs stay yours.

The first is the words. Treat the draft as raw material, not a finished piece. Rewrite it until the choices sound like you.

The second is the facts. Open the source. Find the line that backs your claim. Then write down what you found: it holds up, it says the opposite, or you could not find it.

One safety note before you paste anything into an outside AI app. Take out real names, addresses, private messages, and account details. What you type there leaves LearningAI. Two made-up sentences are enough to practise with.

And checking a source only answers one question: does this page say this? It does not tell you the advice is safe. For health, money, law, or safety, ask a professional or an official page before you act.
steps.mistake: Reading the smooth draft and the tidy source, deciding both jobs are finished, and posting it.
steps.good: Treating the draft as a first pass. Rewrite the words that are not yours. Then open the source and find the exact line.

steps.title: Is this fact settled yet?
steps.prompt: It hands you each of these. Sort them. Is the fact settled, or have you simply not checked it?

items.text: A source with a real-sounding author and year, which you have not opened.
A link you clicked. The article is real, and one sentence in it backs your claim.
'This is well known' with no source named at all.
A real page by the right author, which never actually states the claim.
A page you opened yourself. The publisher checks out and so does the exact line.

steps.reveal: A fact is settled only after you open the source and see three things. It exists. It is by whoever it claims. It says the exact thing. Anything less is unchecked, however convincing the source looks.

steps.title: Draft in your voice, then ask for one real source
steps.prompt: Here is how I actually write. Study it: [paste 2 to 4 sentences you wrote]. Now help me write [the piece]. It has to include this fact: [the fact]. Keep my voice, the same level of formality and my kind of words. After the draft, give me the single best source for that fact: who published it, the exact sentence that backs the claim, and a link. List anything you are not sure is real, so I can check it myself.
steps.note: The writing sample matters, but you can make it up. Take out names, contact details, places, and anything private before pasting into an outside app. Try something like: 'Hey, quick one. I keep meaning to ask about Saturday but life has been wild. Tell me what works and I will sort it.' Then pick something low-stakes, like a four-sentence post for a gardening group, and check its fact on a page you open yourself.

steps.title: The two jobs, in order
steps.goal: Turn the draft into a finished piece that sounds like you and rests on a fact you checked.
correct: Read the draft and circle every word or phrase you would never say.
Rewrite each circled phrase in your own words so the voice is yours.
Actually open the source it gave you.
Run three checks. Does the page exist? Is it by who it says? Does it say the exact thing?
If any check fails, cut the fact, or swap in one you checked yourself.
If the fact touches health, money or law, confirm it with a professional or an official page before acting.
steps.note: Words first, then facts. Skip the first and you sound like nobody. Skip the second and you sound right while being wrong.

steps.title: Do both jobs on something new
steps.question: Take a new piece of writing of your own that needs a fact. You draft it with AI, then finish it yourself. Which of these means you did both jobs?

options.text: I can point to two phrases I put into my own words. I can say what I found at the source, and quote the line that settles it. If it touches health, money or law, I can name who I would ask.
options.feedback: That is both jobs on a new example. The words became yours, and the fact was settled at the source.

options.text: It gave me a clean draft and a source with an author and a link, so the writing is done and the fact holds.
options.feedback: That is the exact trap. A source you did not open proves nothing, and a general draft is not your voice. Both jobs are still waiting.

options.text: I rewrote a few phrases so it sounds like me. The fact came from the AI, so it is probably fine.
options.feedback: You did the words and skipped the facts. It guesses words that fit. Open the source and find the exact line.

options.text: I opened the source. It is real and by the right author. I did not check whether it says my claim.
options.feedback: Real and by the right author is not enough. A genuine page can still never say your sentence. That third check is the one that catches invented sources.

lessons.title: Everyday Wins: Finish the Small Stuff
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I use AI to finish the small messages and plans I keep putting off?
lessons.blurb: Get a draft in ten seconds. Make it sound like you. Then actually send it.

steps.title: The message you keep avoiding
steps.scenario:
You told your friend Sam you would meet on Saturday. Now you have to cancel.

The text has sat unwritten for three days.

It is not hard. You just keep not doing it.
steps.prompt: What matters most here? Sending it fast. Not hurting Sam. Keeping private details out. Finding a new day. Several matter. Which one comes first?

steps.title: A draft is a starting point, not the final word
steps.body:
When AI writes your message, it is not working out what your friendship needs. It has read a huge amount of writing, and it guesses words that fit the facts and tone you gave it.

That is why the draft arrives fast and smooth. It is also why it can sound like nobody, or promise something you cannot do.

You pick the goal. You decide what is true. You decide what stays private. You decide whether sending this could land badly on someone else.

Keep what you type light. Say 'my friend' instead of a name. Say 'Saturday afternoon' instead of your whole week. No addresses, private messages, health details, or other people's business. What you type into an outside app leaves LearningAI.
steps.mistake: Saving AI for big impressive jobs, then pasting whatever it writes straight into the chat, blank voice and all.
steps.good: Pointing it at the tiny thing you have been dreading. Then changing at least one line so it sounds like you before it goes.

steps.title: What actually belongs in the box?
steps.prompt: Sort each one. Is this a small real job it can help you finish, or something to keep out of the chat?

items.text: A text cancelling Saturday with a friend
A short message to a coach or a shift manager saying you will be late
Your friend's home address and full timetable, typed in 'so it is accurate'
A friendly note to a neighbour about when the fence gets fixed
A private health detail you would rather nobody knew, pasted in as background

steps.reveal: Everyday messages are exactly the right size for this. Just keep the facts thin. Who it is to and the timing is plenty. Private details never had to go in to get a good draft.

steps.title: Draft one real thing now
steps.prompt: Help me write [a message I actually need to send]. Here is the situation: [who it is to, and what is true]. Make it sound [the tone] and keep it short. I will change it so it sounds like me.
steps.note: A made-up situation works fine. Never hand over something private just to finish a lesson. Worked example: 'Help me write a text cancelling Saturday. Something came up. I still want to meet next week. Warm and direct. Do not invent an excuse or promise a date. Keep it short.' Read it for anything untrue, rewrite one line in your own words, then decide yourself whether to send it.

steps.title: The five-step move
steps.goal: Get one small real message drafted, make it sound like you, and actually send it.
correct: Name the one small thing that has been nagging you
Give it the facts and the tone you want
Read the draft it writes
Rewrite at least one line in words you would really say out loud
Send the message, or start the plan for real
steps.note: The last two steps keep the decision yours. A good ending might be sending it, saving it, ringing instead, or deciding it needs more care first. It can write words. It cannot carry what happens next.

steps.title: Save where the line sits

fields.label: What it may help draft
fields.placeholder: A low-stakes message with private details left out

fields.label: What stays my decision
fields.placeholder: Whether, when, and how I contact the person

steps.title: Did you actually do it?
steps.question: On a new low-stakes situation, you get a draft with private details left out, and you rewrite it. Which ending shows it helped without taking over the friendship?

options.text: I checked every fact and promise, rewrote the main line in my own words, and then chose to send it, save it, or ring instead, based on how it would land.
options.feedback: Yes. Finishing is a decision with a reason behind it, not a reflex. The words are yours and you thought about the effect.

options.text: The draft was true and warm, so I sent it after fixing the punctuation. I never thought about ringing instead.
options.feedback: True and warm is a good start. How you send it is part of the decision. A text, a call, or waiting can land very differently.

options.text: I rewrote it in my own words and saved it, but left in a promise I am not sure I can keep.
options.feedback: Sounding like you does not fix a promise you might break. Cut it or soften it before you decide anything.

options.text: I took the private details out and sent the short draft exactly as written, because speed mattered most.
options.feedback: Sending counts for something. Pasting it untouched skips the point: change one line so it sounds like you, not like anybody.

lessons.title: Money, Shopping and Travel
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I use AI to weigh up spending real money, without trusting a price it may have got wrong?
lessons.blurb: Let it lay out your choices. Then check the price yourself, on the page that takes your money.

steps.title: The $89 deal that was not
steps.scenario:
You ask for the best cabin bag under $120.

It picks one at $89. But that one cannot be returned. The tougher bag costs $18 more.

Your thumb is over the Buy button.
steps.prompt: Decide your rule before you look again. Cheapest real total. Easiest to return. Toughest. Or not buying yet. Which one wins, and which claim could change your mind?

steps.title: It gives you leads, not a till
steps.body:
It is genuinely good at laying out your choices. It raises the questions you would forget to ask.

But it is not standing in the shop. It has read an enormous amount of writing, and it guesses which words come next. So a price it types is a good guess, not a scanned label.

Some apps really can look at live web pages now. That helps a lot. Even then it can quote a page that is out of date. Or use a sale that ended last week. Or copy a number across wrong.

So people say it 'knows the price' the way a checkout knows a barcode. It does not. It guesses, and sometimes searches, and a search can still miss.

Treat every price, deal and 'in stock' as a lead you go and check.
steps.mistake: You see '$89, on sale', treat it as today's price, and buy. Then $119 comes off your card, because the sale ended last week.
steps.good: You treat the $89 as a lead. You open the shop's own page for that bag and read the real number before spending anything.

steps.title: Checking means the page that takes your money
steps.prompt: Checking means you open the real page yourself. The shop's own page. The airline's booking page. The bank's own rates page. Which of these count as checking a price?

items.text: Opening the shop's own page for that item and reading the price at checkout
Going to the airline's booking page for your dates and seeing the fare
Trusting the number the AI typed in its answer
Reading a 'best deals' blog that lists the sale price
Looking at a photo of the price somebody posted
Checking the number on the company's own prices page

steps.reveal: Trust the page that takes your money. Not a screenshot. Not a deals blog. Not the AI. The actual page where you would tap Buy.

steps.title: Run it on a real decision
steps.prompt: Help me decide on [the thing I want to buy, book, or sign up for]. I can spend [amount and currency]. What matters most to me is [the thing you care about]. Compare [number] choices, with the honest downsides of each for my situation. Then list exactly what I should check myself before I commit, and name the real website where I would check each one. If you can look things up online, say so, and tell me the date on what you found.
steps.note: A made-up or small decision works fine. Stay general. A rounded budget and what you care about is enough. Never your card number, account number, exact income, booking code, home address, or travel dates. What you type into an outside app leaves LearningAI. When it names a price or a rule, open the company's real page yourself before spending.

steps.title: The order that catches the mistake
steps.goal: Make one real decision about money, shopping or travel, and catch at least one wrong price or claim before you spend.
correct: Name the decision you are actually facing right now
Say what you can spend, and the one thing that matters most
Ask it to compare two or three choices, with the honest downsides of each
Ask what it would double-check before spending, and on which real website
Open one of those real pages and confirm the key price or claim yourself
Decide
steps.note: The checking step is the whole point, not a bonus. It narrows the field. The real page confirms the number. For anything you sign, like a loan, insurance or a contract, take the final terms to a qualified person, not to a chat app.

steps.title: Save your check

fields.label: What I am willing to give up
fields.placeholder: Money, time, quality, risk, or being able to change my mind

fields.label: Where I check the deciding claim
fields.placeholder: The real seller, company, timetable, or rules page

steps.title: Did you actually check?
steps.question: Take a new decision you have not used yet. Which of two subscriptions to keep, say, or the cheapest train home next month. Ask for the comparison, then open the real page for ONE price or claim. What lets you say you passed?

options.text: I opened the real page and can finish this sentence. 'It told me the price was ___. On the real page it was ___, so I will or will not trust it.'
options.feedback: That is the skill. You did not guess. You opened the page that takes your money and compared. Match or gap, now you know.

options.text: I checked the price on the shop's page, but not delivery, return fees, or whether it suits what I actually need
options.feedback: The sticker price is settled. The real total and the thing you care about are still open, and either could flip the decision.

options.text: I opened the company's page and confirmed the total, but the page was for different dates and a different version
options.feedback: Right page, wrong item. Match the exact thing, the exact dates and the exact terms before you call a number checked.

options.text: I confirmed both prices on their real pages, then took the cheaper one without thinking about its weaker returns policy
options.feedback: Both prices are checked. Your rule is not finished. Decide whether losing the right to return it is worth the saving.

lessons.title: Health and Other Big Questions
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I use AI to understand something serious, without letting it decide anything for me?
lessons.blurb: Use it to walk in prepared. Understanding is fine. Deciding belongs to a person who is answerable.

steps.title: The very confident answer
steps.scenario:
You have had a headache for three days. You type: what is wrong with me, and what should I take?

Back come three calm paragraphs. They name a likely cause. They suggest a medicine.

It sounds completely sure of itself.
steps.prompt: It never looked at you. It does not know your history. It cannot run a test. So what did you actually just get?

steps.title: Understand. Do not decide.
steps.body:
For serious questions, use AI to understand and to get ready. Not to work out what is wrong, and never to choose what to do.

It is good at turning hard words into plain ones. It is good at building a list of questions to take to somebody qualified.

The line is simple. It has not examined you. It does not know your whole history. It cannot test anything. A smooth answer can still be completely wrong.

So never start, stop or change a medicine because a chat app suggested it. Ask the doctor or pharmacist who is answerable for your care.

Before you use an outside app, take out your name, your date of birth, any record number, a photo of a label, a test result, your full list of symptoms, and anything about somebody else's health. What you type there leaves LearningAI. A made-up or general question works fine for practice.

Do not use AI in an emergency. For chest pain, trouble breathing, or a bad reaction to a medicine, call your local emergency number. If you feel unsafe, or at risk of hurting yourself or anyone else, reach a person you trust, emergency services, or a crisis line. In the United States and its territories, call or text 988.
steps.mistake: Asking what is wrong with you and what to take, then acting on the answer because it sounded certain.
steps.good: Asking it to explain the basics in plain words and build you questions for a real professional. Then deciding nothing on its word alone.

steps.title: Understanding, or deciding?
steps.prompt: The rule. AI can help you understand. A qualified person makes the decision. Sort each one.

items.text: Explain in plain words why a doctor might want to check blood pressure again in a month
Tell me which medicine to take, and how much, for what I am feeling
Help me write a list of questions to ask the pharmacist
Work out what illness I have from how I feel today
Explain what a letter about benefits usually means, so I can follow the meeting
Confirm that it is safe to stop taking a prescribed medicine early

steps.reveal: Everything in the first group keeps you understanding and preparing. Everything in the second is a decision that belongs to a qualified person, however sure the answer sounds.

steps.title: Turn it into a sheet of questions
steps.prompt: I want to understand this and prepare questions. I do not want you to tell me what is wrong or what to do. Here is a made-up, general situation: [the general question, with anything identifying taken out]. Explain the general idea in plain words. Mark clearly what only a qualified [type of professional] can decide. Say where you are unsure. Then write three questions somebody could ask that professional. Do not suggest a medicine, a dose, an illness, or a treatment.
steps.note: Use a made-up or general question, like why a doctor might recheck blood pressure later. Not your own history, and not a document from your account. The professional could be a doctor, pharmacist, nurse, dentist, lawyer or money adviser. Read the explanation back in your own words. Circle one question to actually ask. You should leave with questions, not a verdict.

steps.title: Save your question sheet

fields.label: What I want to understand
fields.placeholder: why a doctor might want to check my blood pressure again in a month

fields.label: Who actually decides this
fields.placeholder: doctor, pharmacist, nurse, lawyer, adviser

fields.label: One question I will ask a real person
fields.placeholder: Is a one-month recheck normal, or is something worrying you?

fields.label: One thing I will not act on until a person confirms it
fields.placeholder: any dose, or any 'you should stop taking this' it suggested

steps.title: Do it on a NEW question
steps.question: Pick a different serious question from the one you just used. What a new prescription is for, or what a letter about benefits means. Run it. Which answer shows you actually did the skill?

options.text: I can say the basics back in my own words with the screen shut. I can point to one question I will ask a real professional. And I can name one thing I will not act on until a person confirms it.
options.feedback: That closes it. You got smarter and stayed in charge. You understood, you prepared, and the decision stayed with somebody answerable.

options.text: I used a general question and prepared three good ones, but I also planned to change a dose before speaking to anybody.
options.feedback: Calm and complete is exactly how a confident mistake reads. It cannot examine you. Use its answer to build questions and let a professional decide.

options.text: I can explain the general idea and I named a professional. I also pasted in my full test result to get sharper questions.
options.feedback: The preparation was good. The test result crossed the line. Keep the question general and take the actual document straight to the professional.

lessons.title: Thinking Partner, Not Answer Machine
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I finish smarter, instead of just holding an answer I cannot explain?
lessons.blurb: The best thing you get from AI is not the answer. It is your own thinking pushed further than you would push it alone.

steps.title: You have the answer. Are you any smarter?
steps.scenario:
You are stuck on a real choice. Say, whether to take the harder class next year.

You type it in, read the tidy answer, and go with it.

A week later a friend asks why you chose it. You can repeat its reasons. You cannot actually explain them.
steps.prompt: What do you need from help here? More choices. A challenge to something you assumed. A missing fact. Or the decision itself. Which of those should stay yours?

steps.title: Why 'partner' is a way of using it, not a claim about it
steps.body:
The thing answering you has read an enormous amount of writing. It guesses which words come next.

Nothing in that checks whether the words are true. So a genuinely good idea and a confident mistake come out looking exactly the same.

Calling it a thinking partner is about how you use it. It does not think, and it does not care what you decide.

You create the value, in three ways. You write down your own view first. You choose which facts actually matter. You keep the decision.

This is the same split as 'do my homework for me' versus 'I am stuck on question 4, walk me through it'. The first hands over the part that was supposed to teach you. The second keeps it.

If you use an outside app, pick a small or made-up decision. Take out names, your school or job, amounts of money, private messages, health details, and anything about somebody else. What you type there leaves LearningAI.
steps.mistake: Asking the lazy way, reading the answer, and deciding that because it could answer, there was no point thinking about it yourself.
steps.good: Asking in a way that makes you reason first. Then you leave understanding it, not just holding it.

steps.title: Handing it over, or keeping it?
steps.prompt: Each line is something you might type. Does it hand the thinking over, or keep you in it?

items.text: Just tell me. Harder class or easier class?
Do not answer yet. First ask me two questions about how I am thinking about this.
Write my whole conclusion so I can paste it in.
After I reply, name one thing I am assuming that might not be true.
Give me the final answer in one sentence.

steps.reveal: The lines that keep you thinking all make you produce something before it gives its view. That is the whole move. Not cleverer software. A request that will not let you skip the thinking.

steps.title: Run it on something you are actually chewing on
steps.prompt: I want to think through [a real question or choice], not just be handed the answer. Do not answer yet. First ask me [2 or 3] questions about how I am currently thinking about it. After I reply, name [one thing I seem to be missing: a blind spot, a shaky assumption, an angle I skipped]. Then let me have another go before you give your own view.
steps.note: Worked example: 'I want to think through whether to join a weekend repair project or keep that time free. Do not decide for me. Ask two questions, name one thing I am assuming, and name one fact I should check.' Use a small or made-up situation with nothing identifying in it. Answer the questions yourself. Check any fact the decision leans on. Write your reason down before you read its view.

steps.title: Save it as a line you can reuse

fields.label: The question or the choice
fields.placeholder: whether to take the harder class next year

fields.label: How many questions it asks me first
The gap I want it to find
fields.placeholder: one thing I am assuming that might not be true

steps.title: Prove it on a brand-new question
steps.question: Pick a completely different question from the one you just ran. When can you say you did the skill?

options.text: I answered its questions myself before it gave any view. And I can name one specific thing I now understand because I worked it out.
options.feedback: That is it. You stayed in the loop. You can explain it in your own words instead of repeating its words.

options.text: It showed me two choices and one hidden assumption. I picked the quickest choice without checking whether the assumption was true.
options.feedback: It widened the view. Your decision still rests on something unchecked. Check the fact it leans on, then write your own reason.

options.text: I wrote my own conclusion, but it mostly repeats its reasons, and I cannot say which fact changed my mind.
options.feedback: Then you have a conclusion and you are no smarter. The point is that you can explain it afterwards.

options.text: I compared its view with my first view, but I treated the links it gave as checked without opening them.
options.feedback: Sounding sure and having links is not the same as being right. It guesses words that fit. Open anything the decision depends on.

lessons.title: Draft, Pick It Apart, Do It Again
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I get genuinely better work out of AI, by going round the loop instead of asking once?
lessons.blurb: Good work comes from going round again. Draft it, have it picked apart, fix it yourself, repeat.

steps.title: The rough first go
steps.scenario:
You need three sentences inviting people to something. A games night, a litter pick, a club.

Your first go is clear but dull. Nobody would come because of it.

Sending it now takes ten seconds. Fixing it might actually fill the room.
steps.prompt: Before you change a single word, pick three tests it has to pass. Clear? Honest? Sounds like you? Useful? Gets a reply? And how would you know it improved?

steps.title: The quality is in the loop, not the first draft
steps.body:
Good work comes from going round. Draft it. Hold it against your tests. Fix it. Test it again.

When AI 'picks apart' your draft, it is guessing sensible-sounding comments from the tests you gave it. It does not know what is genuinely good. It has no idea how your friends will react.

So some of its comments will be sharp and useful. Some will flatten your voice or miss the point entirely.

You set the tests. You decide which comments are right. You are allowed to say no, as long as you can say why.

If you use an outside app, take out real names, addresses, private messages, unpublished school or work material, and anything about another person. What you type there leaves LearningAI. A made-up draft is fine.
steps.mistake: Binning the first draft the moment it is not great, and asking for a total rewrite instead.
steps.good: Keeping the draft. Writing down what good actually means here. Then going round the loop twice.

steps.title: Go round twice
steps.goal: Turn a rough draft into something clearly better, measured against tests you wrote yourself.
correct: Write something short and imperfect yourself. Do not polish it
Write down 3 tests for what good means here, each one you can actually check
Ask it to pick your draft apart against those three tests. Not to rewrite it
You fix it yourself, then paste the new version back
Ask it to pick the new version apart too. That is round two
Put your first draft next to your last one and see how far it climbed
steps.note: You do the rewriting, not the app. It guesses where your words miss your tests. The judgement and the writing stay yours. That is the same line as 'walk me through question 4' rather than 'do it for me'.

steps.title: Ask it to pick your draft apart
steps.prompt: Here is my draft of [what it is]: [paste your draft]. Do NOT rewrite it. Pick it apart against three tests I am setting: 1) [test one], 2) [test two], 3) [test three]. For each test, tell me one thing that works and the single most important fix. Keep it short. I will fix it myself and paste the new version back for a second round.
steps.note: Make each test something you can actually check. For example: the time and the thing to do are clear in one read. It uses words I would say out loud. It promises nothing I cannot deliver. Use a made-up invitation, listing, instruction card, or note, with names and details taken out. After each round, accept one suggestion, reject one and say why, and make the change yourself.

steps.title: Save your three tests

fields.label: What I am writing
fields.placeholder: 3 sentences inviting people to my robotics club

fields.label: Test 1, something I can check
fields.placeholder: clear on a single read

fields.label: Test 2, something I can check
fields.placeholder: sounds like a real person, not a leaflet

fields.label: Test 3, something I can check
fields.placeholder: makes somebody actually want to turn up

steps.title: Prove you have the loop
steps.question: Pick something new you did not use above. Write 3 tests, go round twice, then say which test drove each change. Which of these means you have it?

options.text: For every change between my first draft and my last, I can point to the exact test it was serving.
options.feedback: That is it. If you can name the test behind each change on a fresh piece, you own the loop, not one lucky answer.

options.text: The second version is smoother and shorter, but it dropped a detail people actually need.
options.feedback: Smoother is not the test. Better means better against the tests you wrote, and you should be able to name which one each change served.

options.text: I passed two tests, then changed the third one halfway through without writing down why.
options.feedback: Changing a test can be the right call. Write down the reason and hold the earlier draft against the new test too. Otherwise you cannot see what improved.

lessons.title: Planning a Big Project Together
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I turn something too big to start into a plan I actually own?
lessons.blurb: Feeling stuck is usually a planning problem, not a you problem. Cut the mountain into stairs, then pick the first one.

steps.title: The thing you keep not starting
steps.scenario:
There is a project you keep not starting. A big family get-together. Moving house. A long essay.

It feels too big to even begin.

So it sits there, getting heavier every week you look at it.
steps.prompt: What must the plan protect first? The deadline. The money. Somebody else's time. Safety. Your own energy. Which of those can bend, and which cannot?

steps.title: It cuts the mountain into stairs. You decide where they go.
steps.body:
Feeling stuck is usually a planning problem, not a failure of character.

AI is fast at chopping a big thing into ordinary stages. That is genuinely useful when you cannot see the first step.

But it does not know your calendar. Or your money. Or how tired you are. Or what you are allowed to do. Or who else this lands on.

Where it does not know, it fills the gap with a sensible guess. That is what it does.

So you become the editor. You supply the real facts. You cut the stages you do not need. You move steps around. And you add a point where somebody has to say yes before money is spent, a booking is made, something is published, or another person gets pulled in.

Before an outside app sees any of this, swap names for roles, round the money, keep places vague, and cut addresses, account numbers, timetables, private messages, and anything about somebody else. What you type there leaves LearningAI.
steps.mistake: Treating its plan as finished and true, and just following it, as though it knew your actual life.
steps.good: Treating yourself as the editor, not the audience. You add the real facts it can only guess at, then cut and reorder.

steps.title: Ask it to plan a real project
steps.prompt: Help me plan [the big project]. Here is my real situation: [deadline / what I already have / what is blocking me]. Break it into [4 to 6] stages, and for each stage give me the very first small step. Then suggest one point where I should stop and decide again before carrying on. If something important is missing, ask me. Do not guess it.
steps.note: Worked example: 'Help me plan a family get-together in about three months. I have a rough number of guests but no venue, and money is the hard limit. Use five stages, and add a point where I approve before anything gets booked.' Use facts that matter but do not identify anyone. A community event, tidying a room, a repair, a move, or something you want to build all work. It suggests. You approve anything that commits you.

steps.title: Be the editor
steps.goal: Turn its plan into a plan you own, and start it today.
correct: Write down three honest facts: your deadline, what you already have, what is blocking you
Ask it to break the goal into stages, with a first step for each
Cross out one stage you do not actually need
Move one step earlier or later, because you know your life and it does not
Add one point where you or the person affected says yes, before money, booking, publishing, or anything you cannot undo
Circle the single first step, and write down what time today you will do it
steps.note: The cutting and moving is the whole point. It produces an ordinary plan for an ordinary version of this job. You are the one who knows the real facts it cannot see.

steps.title: Save your plan

fields.label: The project
fields.placeholder: e.g. organise a get-together for 30 people

fields.label: My single first step, today
fields.placeholder: e.g. message 3 people to find some possible dates

fields.label: What time today I will do it
fields.placeholder: e.g. after dinner, 7pm

fields.label: Where I stop and decide again
fields.placeholder: e.g. once I have a price for the room, check the money before booking

steps.title: Do you own the plan?
steps.question: Take a different heavy project you have not touched. Run the same request. Edit it: cut one stage, move one step, add one stopping point. Then say your first step out loud, and why. What proves you own it?

options.text: I can say my first step AND why I chose it, without reading its answer again
options.feedback: That is ownership. The plan is in your head now, not just on the screen, and you know why you are starting there.

options.text: I cut a stage and picked a first step, but the approval point still comes after the money is gone
options.feedback: You edited the plan. The stopping point sits after the thing you cannot undo. Move it before the spending or the booking.

options.text: I reordered the stages to fit my week, but I never asked the other people whether the new timing works
options.feedback: The timing can suit you and still fail everyone else. Ask them before you lock it in.

options.text: I can name the first step and my reason, but the reason rests on a price I have not checked
options.feedback: Your reasoning is clear, and it stands on an unchecked number. Confirm that before you commit to anything.

lessons.title: Hand Over the Work, Keep the Calls
lessons.coreQuestion: Which parts of a real job can I hand over, and which parts have to stay mine?
lessons.blurb: Hand over the typing and the first draft. Keep the calls only you should be making.

steps.title: Writing up what everyone did
steps.scenario:
A group project needs a fair write-up of what three people contributed.

That job is really four jobs. Gathering what actually happened. Finding good words. Deciding what is true and fair about each person. Getting it into the right format.

You open a chat app to speed it up.
steps.prompt: Which of those four would you be uneasy handing over completely? And why that one?

steps.title: Hand over the work. Keep the calls.
steps.body:
Someone good at this does not hand over as much as possible. They protect the parts that land on people.

AI can draft, sort and format. It cannot know what actually happened in your group. It cannot ask anyone if that is okay. It cannot weigh a friendship. And it carries nothing if it goes wrong.

So keep a part yourself when any of these is true. It has to be true. It carries what you believe. It affects somebody. Somebody else has to agree to it. It goes out with your name on it.

Hand over the rest, but only work you can undo, and only if you are going to read it before it goes anywhere.

Before an outside app sees anything, take out names, contact details, private messages, anything about how somebody is performing, and anything belonging to another person. What you type there leaves LearningAI.
steps.mistake: Typing 'write the reviews for my three teammates' and pasting the answer straight in.
steps.good: Letting it find warm wording from YOUR notes, while you decide what is true and fair about each person. And keeping private details about named people on your side of the line.

steps.title: Run the keep test
steps.prompt: Sort each part. Hand over means typing, drafting, formatting, sorting, and you still read it. Keep means it has to be true about real people, it carries what you believe, or your name is on it.

Decide what each person actually did well this year
Put the finished text into the right format
Judge whether the tone is fair and even across all three
Cut a long project document down to three bullet points
Decide which private details about a named person go in

steps.reveal: The hand-over parts are labour. Drafting, formatting, shortening. You still read them before they go. The keep parts all pass the same test: they must be true about real people, or your name is on the call. It cannot check what your teammates did, even with the whole web open. So what happened, and what is fair, stay yours.

steps.title: Get the map of parts
steps.prompt: Here is a job I need to do: [your job]. Break it into its separate parts. For each part, say whether I should hand it to you or do it myself. Flag any part where my own judgement, my values, or what I know about real people matters, and explain why in one line. Do not do the job yet. Just give me the map.
steps.note: Use a real or made-up job with several parts. Planning a meal, an event, a games night, a handover at work, a repair, an application, a group project. Give it nothing that identifies anyone. Then hand it one part you could undo, keep one part yourself, and write down who has to approve before anything is sent, posted, booked, marked, or paid for.

lessons.title: Keeping Your Voice and Being Honest
lessons.coreQuestion: When AI helps me write, how do I stay the real writer and stay honest about the help?
lessons.blurb: Edit it back into your own words. Then decide who needs to know that AI helped.

steps.title: The line that is not yours
steps.scenario:
You ask an app to tidy up a thank-you note to a teacher.

Back comes this. 'I am profoundly grateful for the invaluable investment you have made in my growth.'

It reads well. You would never say 'profoundly' out loud in your life.
steps.prompt: If you sent that as it is, whose words did your teacher actually get? Would you be comfortable saying you wrote it?

steps.title: Two moves, one habit
steps.body:
Most real work mixes your effort with some kind of tool. That is normal. What matters is that somebody stands behind the claims, the choices and the final words.

You stay the writer with two moves.

First, make the words sound like you. Read it out loud. Anything you would never say, rewrite.

Second, say that AI helped, when the person reading it would want to know. A teacher, a customer, a rule, an audience.

Before an outside app sees a sample of your writing, take out names, addresses, private messages, confidential work, and anything about somebody else. What you type there leaves LearningAI. Made-up samples work fine.

It can suggest wording. You approve every claim, and you decide what honesty looks like here.
steps.mistake: Pasting the smooth draft, sending it, and either claiming you wrote it alone or never mentioning the help.
steps.good: Reading it out loud, rewriting every line that is not yours, then deciding whether this particular reader needs one line saying AI helped.

steps.title: Which situation are you in?
steps.prompt: Whether to say so depends on the situation. Sort each one. Rough rule: say so when somebody is relying on who wrote it or on it being right. For tidying up your own writing, usually nobody needs a note.

items.text: A school essay where AI is allowed, but you must say how you used it
A report for a customer, where the numbers and who wrote them matter
Something creative you are posting publicly that AI helped shape
Turning your own scrappy notes into a tidy list, for yourself
A quick personal draft you are going to rewrite completely anyway

steps.reveal: When the rule is unclear, do not guess. Ask the teacher or your manager BEFORE you submit. Guessing is the actual risk here. And never claim you did it all alone if AI shaped it.

steps.title: Teach it your voice, then ask it to be straight with you
steps.prompt: Here is how I actually write. Study it: [paste 3 or 4 sentences you wrote]. Now help me improve [the new piece], keeping my voice. Same level of formality, my kind of words, nothing fancier than I would say. Then do two things. One, list every phrase you added that does not sound like me. Two, tell me honestly what kind of help this was: ideas, editing, or mostly written by you. I need that so I can describe it accurately.
steps.note: Use three made-up or already-public sentences in your style. You do not need a private sample. Take out anything identifying or confidential. Try a thank-you note, an item for sale, a club announcement, a caption, or an application. Then accept or reject each phrase it suggested, and write your honest one-liner before anything gets shared.

lessons.title: Write It Once, Reuse It Forever
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I turn a request I type over and over into a saved recipe where only one thing changes?
lessons.blurb: Stop retyping the same request. Write the steps once, and swap in the new bit each time.

steps.title: The third time this week
steps.scenario:
For the third time this week you type almost the same request.

Turn this shopping list, or this repair checklist, or these meeting notes, into the same tidy format.

Same instructions. New stuff. Every single time.
steps.prompt: What part of that request actually changes each time you send it? What part is word for word the same?

steps.title: A fixed step, or the new bit?
steps.prompt: You keep asking it to turn meeting notes into a to-do list. Sort each piece. Is it one of the steps that never change, or the new stuff you paste in each time?

items.text: "Pull out every job as its own line."
This week's messy notes, pasted in.
"For each job, add who is doing it and any deadline mentioned."
"Lay the answer out as a checklist with empty [ ] boxes."
The names and dates from today's meeting.

steps.reveal: The instructions are identical every time. Only the notes change. That gap is the whole trick. Write the fixed part once, and mark the changing part as one clear slot.

steps.title: A recipe you only write once
steps.body:
Here is the idea. Take a job you do again and again. Write it as numbered steps, with one blank slot for the thing that changes. Then you only ever fill the blank.

People call that a workflow. It is just a recipe with one changing ingredient.

Reusing it saves real time. It also repeats your mistakes. A bad step, or a careless habit with private stuff, now happens every single run.

So before an outside app sees anything, take out real names, addresses, timetables, contact details, account details, private messages, confidential documents, and anything about another person. What you type there leaves LearningAI. Made-up material works fine for practice.

And put a stop in it. Before anything gets sent, posted, booked, deleted, bought, or used to judge a person, you read it and say yes.
steps.mistake: Retyping the whole request from scratch every time, explaining the same instructions you have already explained ten times.
steps.good: Writing the fixed instructions once as numbered steps. Marking the one changing part [INPUT], which just means the bit you paste in fresh.

steps.title: Build the reusable version
steps.goal: Turn a request you keep retyping into a saved recipe with one blank slot.
correct: Find a job you ask for more than once. Same job, different details.
Split the part that NEVER changes, the steps, from the part that ALWAYS changes, the new bit.
Write the fixed part as numbered steps that would work for ANY version of this job, not just today's.
Mark the one changing part clearly as [INPUT].
Run it once on made-up material, and check the answer against your own rule for good enough.
Run it again on something different, then add a stop where a person says yes before anything real happens.
steps.note: The proof is the second run. If you only had to change the [INPUT] and both answers came out the same shape, you built something reusable. If you found yourself rewriting a step, that step was secretly part of the changing bit. Move it into the slot.

steps.title: Run yours twice
steps.prompt:
This is a saved recipe I will reuse. Follow these numbered steps every time, in order. Only the INPUT changes each run.
Steps:
1. [step one, what to do first]
2. [step two, what to do next]
3. [step three, how to lay it out or finish]
How the answer should look: [describe it]
INPUT: [paste the one thing that changes this run]
steps.note: Use made-up material first, or take the details out. Swap names for roles and drop anything private or confidential. Run it twice. Compare both answers against the same rule for good enough. Add 'STOP AND ASK ME' before anything is sent, posted, booked, deleted, bought, or used to judge somebody. For health, money, law or safety, only use it to prepare questions, and take the decision to a qualified person.
