options.feedback: Yes. The second run on fresh material is the proof. Same steps, new bit, same shape of answer.

options.text: Save it in the app's memory and assume future material will be as safe as the first lot.
options.feedback: Memory is not a safety net. Save it somewhere you control, check what the app keeps, and clean each new piece of material before you paste it.

options.text: Rewrite a few of the fixed steps for the second run, but keep calling it the same recipe.
options.feedback: Then it is a one-off request again. The steps should fit any version of this job. If a step only fits today, it belongs in the slot.

options.text: Assume it works, because the first run looked good.
options.feedback: One good run proves nothing about the next one. Run it on a second, different piece without touching the steps. That is the real test.

lessons.title: Designing and Making
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I design a tiny tool with AI, test it properly, and still understand what I made?
lessons.blurb: Start with one small annoyance. Test the case where it breaks. Keep a way back to what worked.

steps.title: The impressive thing you cannot undo
steps.scenario:
You ask for a shortcut, and back comes something that looks finished. Maybe some code. Maybe a spreadsheet formula.

You cannot explain what it does. You have not tried feeding it anything strange. You do not know how to get back to the version that worked.

Pointing it at your real files would turn a bit of learning into a gamble.
steps.prompt: What would you need to understand, test, and be able to undo before this thing was allowed near anything real?

steps.title: 'It runs' is the start, not the finish
steps.body:
You do not have to run any code to do this lesson.

Pick the safest route that works on whatever you already own. Sketch the screens on paper. Write it as a checklist. Lay out an empty spreadsheet. Describe one page in words.

Those are real work, not the easy option. A rough first version on paper tells you more than code you cannot read.

If you do want code, only use a throwaway space in your browser that cannot touch your files. Nothing installed. No passwords. No accounts. No real documents.

Then, whichever route you took: save a copy that works before every change. Try one ordinary made-up example. Try one deliberately awkward one. And write down how you get back to the good copy before you run anything.

For this lesson, never let it into your folders, contacts, payments, messages, or anything that can post or delete.
steps.mistake: Pasting code or formulas into something real first, and planning to work out the risks afterwards.
steps.good: Making the smallest version you can, guessing where it will break, testing it with made-up examples, and proving you can get back.

steps.title: Which annoyance fits a tiny tool?
steps.prompt: A tiny tool suits a small job that keeps coming back and has a clear finish. Sort each annoyance. Good fit, or too big and vague?
buckets: Good fit for a tiny tool

items.text: Every week I add up my spending by hand and it takes ages
I want a suggested naming plan for six made-up file names, without touching a real folder
I want a paper sketch of one page with a made-up name, a box for a picture, and a button
I want to sort my whole life out and get more done
Build me an app that does everything my company needs
A little scoreboard that counts points on games night

steps.reveal: The good fits are small, repeating and specific. You can picture exactly what finished looks like. Huge or vague goals have no smallest version, so shrink them first. Name one annoyance you could describe in a single sentence.

steps.title: Design the smallest safe version
steps.prompt: The small annoyance that keeps coming back is: [describe it, without pasting any real data]. Help me make the smallest useful version. First offer me three routes. A, a checklist or a paper sketch. B, an empty spreadsheet or a layout with no code. C, code only if I already have a throwaway browser space. I choose route [A, B or C]. For my route, give me four things. What goes in, what comes out, and three steps or fewer. One ordinary made-up test and one awkward one. A clear way to tell whether it passed. And the exact step that gets me back to the good copy. Do not ask me to install anything, sign in, hand over any access, or use real files. Stop after the plan so I can explain each part before anything gets made.
steps.note: Routes A and B finish this activity completely, on a phone or on paper. Route C is optional, and must stay inside a throwaway browser space with no downloads and no access to your things. If you have no safe space, do not run code. Hand in the tested design and your way back instead.

steps.title: Make it, then prove you understand it
steps.goal: Turn an annoyance that keeps coming back into a small version you understand, can test, and can undo.
correct: Name one small annoyance that keeps coming back, without typing in anything real or private
Pick the safest route: paper or checklist, empty spreadsheet or no-code layout, or an optional throwaway browser space
Before building, write what goes in, what comes out, how you will know it passed, what it may touch, and how you get back
Save a copy that works, then test one ordinary made-up example and one awkward one
Explain each part, and compare what happened with what you expected
Change one thing you can undo, test again, and go back if it fails
steps.note: It is ready for learning when you can explain it, test it, and put it back. Running generated code on something real is not required, and it proves nothing about whether you understand it.

steps.title: Prove you understand it
steps.question: For a NEW annoyance, what is the strongest sign that you actually understand the thing you designed?

options.text: It ran without any errors, so I understand it
options.feedback: Running is the start, not the finish. It proves the thing works today. A block you cannot read will break in ways you cannot fix.

options.text: I can explain the parts. I can show an ordinary test and an awkward one. I can say what one change will do, and get back to the good copy if it fails
options.feedback: Exactly. Explaining it, testing it, changing it safely, and getting back. Paper, spreadsheet, no-code or a throwaway browser space can all meet that.

options.text: It said this was beginner-friendly. So I ran it on my real files, with no way back
options.feedback: Being told it is simple is not the same as understanding it. The test is whether you can explain the parts and say what a change will do.

options.text: I added more features first. I never decided how to tell whether the smallest version worked
options.feedback: More features make it bigger and harder to understand, not better. Aim for the smallest thing you genuinely grasp.

lessons.title: What It Is Allowed To Touch
lessons.coreQuestion: When AI can do things for me, how do I stay in charge of what it can see and change?
lessons.blurb: Give it the least it needs. Written promises are not locks, so look for controls you can actually see.

steps.title: 'I can tidy your files for you'
steps.scenario:
A made-up helper offers to tidy a practice folder.

A chat app only writes back. This one takes several steps by itself and uses other software to do them. People call that an agent.

This exercise shows you five powers it could be given. Your job is not to decide whether it seems clever. Your job is to decide what it should be allowed to touch.
steps.prompt: The question is not 'is it smart?' It is 'what can it actually reach?' What would you want to be sure it cannot touch before it starts?

steps.title: Choose what it can touch
steps.goal: In this made-up run, it may organise six invented files inside a practice folder called 'Demo Trip'. Pick the smallest set of powers that still lets it rename and group things in a way you can undo. No real folder is connected to anything here.

tools.name: Read the six invented file names inside 'Demo Trip'
Show me the renames and folders it suggests, before anything happens
Delete any file it decides is a copy
Read every other folder on your computer
Move files out of 'Demo Trip' to somewhere else

steps.note: This is a list of powers, not a set of instructions. Least access means the software simply cannot do the things you did not tick. Nothing here ever reaches a real folder, photo, email or account.

steps.title: Least access, and a stop sign you can see
steps.body:
Before you let anything act for you, decide three things. What it may LOOK at. What it may CHANGE. And what it must ASK you about first.

One word, plainly. Permission just means you letting something do a thing. Real permission lives in the app's settings or your device's settings, where you can see it and take it back.

Here is the part people get wrong. Typing 'please do not delete anything' is a request, not a lock. If the power is switched on, the request is all that stands in the way.

So look for four things you can actually see. A practice run on made-up files first. A visible list of what it did. A point where a person says yes, before anything is sent, posted, bought, deleted, overwritten, moved or shared. And a way to switch its access off.

One privacy rule. Do not connect an outside helper to your real accounts, messages, contacts, photos or files just to finish a lesson. Both your information and that access can leave LearningAI.

If you cannot see a permission, and cannot take it back, do not grant it.
steps.mistake: Giving it access to everything, hoping it behaves, and walking away while it runs.
steps.good: Switching most of its powers off. Trying it on made-up files. Making it wait for your yes, and keeping the record. And refusing the run when those things are missing.

steps.title: A real lock, or just a promise?
steps.prompt: Sort each protection. A real lock stops the action happening. A promise only asks it to behave, and cannot prove the action is impossible.
buckets: A real limit you can see

items.text: A practice space that shows only six invented file names and is joined to nothing else on the device
The instruction says 'please do not look anywhere else'
Every rename shows up in a list first, and nothing happens until a person approves it
It says 'I promise I will pause before deleting anything'
Deleting is simply not one of the powers it has, and the practice space has a reset that works

steps.reveal: Words tell it what you want. They are not permissions. The proof looks different. The power is switched off. You can see what it did. A person has to approve. You can take access back, and you can undo. If an app cannot show you those, use the made-up version and give it nothing real.

steps.title: Put the order in your favour

correct: Look at the list of powers and tick only reading inside the practice folder and showing renames first
Refuse deleting, reading the whole device, and moving anything out of the invented folder
Write down what a real app would have to offer: a practice run, a visible record, a yes from a person, a pause, a way to take access back, and a way to undo
Go and check the real app's screens and help pages for those things, instead of assuming your instructions created them
If any of them is missing, keep this on paper, and connect no real account or folder
steps.note: Choosing the powers and writing the plan is the whole exercise. It teaches you what to demand from a real product. It does not claim LearningAI ran or checked any of it.

lessons.title: Build One Small Thing That Lasts
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I turn everything I have learned into one small tool I will actually use again?
lessons.blurb: Build it in three stages you can save. Design it, test it where it hurts, then keep proof of what changed.

steps.title: The Tuesday test
steps.scenario:
This whole course has been doing, not reading.

Now think of one annoying job that comes back every single week. Turning messy notes into a revision sheet. Digging out what actually needs a reply. Planning meals around what is already in the cupboard.
steps.prompt: What is ONE job like that you would genuinely want to hand over? The kind of thing you would open again next Tuesday.

steps.title: It is small on purpose
steps.body:
This is your final build. A capstone just means the one thing you make at the end to show what you can do.

It is not a longer request. It is one small tool that survives being used a second time.

Build it in three stages, and save after each one. Stopping after any stage is fine.

STAGE 1, design, about 5 to 10 minutes. Write the numbered steps, one clear blank slot for the thing that changes, what counts as good enough, and what it is allowed to touch.

STAGE 2, test, about 10 to 15 minutes. Run it on one ordinary made-up example. Then on one deliberately awkward made-up example.

STAGE 3, proof, about 10 minutes. Save a before and after, one note about what broke and what you changed, and one fact you checked yourself.

Paper counts. A checklist counts. A block of text you reuse counts. An empty spreadsheet counts. Code is optional, and so is any outside app.

Do not paste in real names, addresses, messages, account details, confidential material, or anything about another person. If your tool affects other people, tell them AI helped when they would want to know. Anything serious still ends with a person who is answerable.
steps.mistake: Deciding a real AI tool has to be huge and impressive, so you never build one. Or building it and trusting whatever comes out.
steps.good: Picking one boring, repeating job. Writing it as reusable steps with one blank slot. Adding a stop if it can affect anything real. Then testing it and checking the facts yourself.

steps.title: Put the build in order
steps.goal: Build a small tool you will reuse, one stage at a time.
correct: Name the repeating job, what you will feed it, what you want back, and what counts as good enough
Have it write the whole thing as numbered steps with ONE clearly marked blank slot
Write what it may look at or change, and add a person's yes before anything real or hard to undo
Run it on one ordinary made-up example and keep a before and after
Run it again on one deliberately awkward example, and fix the worst break
Check the facts against what you actually know, then name your tool and save it
steps.note: Both tests use safe made-up material. First an ordinary example, then an awkward one. You never need a real person's details to prove something is reusable. Save after each stage, so a 35-minute build can be split across a few sittings.

steps.title: Build yours now
steps.prompt:
I am building one small tool in three stages I can save. It might end up as steps on paper, a checklist, a block of text I reuse, an empty spreadsheet, a layout with no code, or an optional small digital version kept somewhere safe.
The repeating job, described with nothing private in it: [your job].
An ordinary made-up example to feed it: [safe example].
What I want back: [the result].
Good enough means: [one thing I can actually check].
STAGE 1. Write the numbered steps with ONE blank slot, what it is allowed to touch, and the point where a person has to say yes. Then stop so I can save it.
STAGE 2. Run those same steps on my ordinary example, then on this awkward one: [awkward example]. Say what broke worst, and suggest one change. Then stop again.
STAGE 3. Help me write a short record: before, after, what broke, what I changed, the result, and one fact I have to go and check myself. Do not ask me to connect an account, install anything, or hand over a real message, a real file, or anybody else's details.
steps.note: You do not need an outside app. You can write all three stages here or on paper and compare them with the examples. If you do use one, only put in made-up text, or text with the details taken out. Save the three stages so your proof does not depend on memory or on one long sitting.

fields.placeholder: e.g. ask me before saving over a file or emailing anyone, or 'text only'

fields.label: What broke, what I changed, what I checked

steps.title: Prove you built a tool
steps.question: You built it. What shows it is a real tool you can reuse, rather than one good answer?

options.text: A fresh made-up example works without rebuilding anything. The limits and the human yes still hold. I saved a before and after, plus one break and my fix. And I checked one fact myself.
options.feedback: That is your graduation. Paper, text, spreadsheet, no-code or careful code all count. Reusing it, testing it, fixing a break and checking a fact are what make it real.

options.text: It gave polished results on two examples, but I never wrote down what it could reach, or where a person says yes.
options.feedback: Two good results show some reuse. There is still no safety line. Write what it may touch and where a person approves before you call it done.

options.text: The result came out in exactly the format I wanted, so I took that as proof the facts were right.
options.feedback: The right shape is not the same as the right facts. Go and check the claim the whole thing rests on, and keep that check with the result.

options.text: You rewrote the whole thing from scratch to handle the new example.
options.feedback: If you rebuild it every time, nothing was saved. A real tool swaps the blank slot and reuses the same steps.

lessons.title: Teach Someone Else
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I know I can explain an AI idea clearly, correctly, and in my own words?
lessons.blurb: Teach one idea by writing, by a private recording, by a simulation with a made-up learner, or to a willing listener. The proof is the same either way.

steps.title: The explanation you can defend
steps.scenario:
You have learned a lot here.

But could you explain one idea in under two minutes, with no clever words? And then handle a fair question about it?

You can prove that on your own. In writing. In a recording nobody else sees. To a made-up learner. Or to a real person, if one happens to be around.
steps.prompt: Which ONE thing you learned would you most want somebody to understand about AI? Write it or say it in a single sentence, now.

steps.title: If you can teach it, you own it
steps.body:
Explaining something out loud shows you whether you actually understand it. There is nowhere to hide.

Four routes count the same. Write a short explanation and answer a hard question you set yourself. Record yourself and keep it on your own device. Explain it to a made-up learner. Or teach a real person who is happy to listen.

Whichever route you take, include four things. One true idea. One thing it cannot do. One example you checked. And one choice that stays with the person listening.

If you involve a real person, ask first. Make it easy for them to stop. Use a made-up example. And never type their name or their reply into an outside app.

Being corrected is proof that you were listening. It is not failure.
steps.mistake: Telling yourself you are still a beginner, so you have nothing to teach. Or teaching a cartoon: 'it just autocompletes' sells it short, and 'it thinks like a person' is wrong.
steps.good: Pick one true idea and explain it plainly to somebody one step behind you. 'It has read a huge amount of writing and guesses the words that fit next. So it can sound totally sure and still be wrong. Check anything that matters.'

steps.title: Is that the honest version?
steps.prompt: You are working out how to explain AI to a friend. Sort each way of putting it. Does it teach the real thing, or bend it?

items.text: It read an enormous amount of human writing, and guesses what is likely to come next.
It is just fancy autocomplete, nothing more.
It thinks and reasons the way a person does.
It can sound completely sure and still be wrong, so check anything that matters.
It is basically magic. Nobody really knows how it works.

steps.reveal: The honest version is: it guesses the words most likely to come next. That beats the put-down and the hype. When you teach, teach the real thing.

steps.title: Pick your route
steps.prompt: I will show I understand this by [writing it down / recording myself and keeping it / explaining it to a made-up learner / teaching somebody who is happy to listen]. The one idea is: [idea]. Help me plan a two-minute explanation with four things: plain words, one made-up example, one honest thing it cannot do, and one choice the listener keeps. Then give me one doubting but fair question. I will answer it in my own words and fix my explanation if I need to.
steps.note: All four routes count the same. No real person, upload, account, or outside app is needed. If you record yourself, keep it private, and delete it afterwards if you would rather. If you pick a listener, ask first, and never record or paste their reply anywhere.

steps.title: From idea to an explanation that holds
steps.goal: Teach one AI idea, using whichever route works for you.
correct: Pick the ONE thing you would most want a friend to know. One idea, not five.
Choose your route: writing, a recording you keep, a made-up learner, or a willing listener.
Explain it in plain words, with one made-up example, one thing it cannot do, and one choice the listener keeps.
Answer one doubting but fair question in your own words.
Fix anything unclear or wrong, then say the whole thing once more.
Save only the idea you cleared up and the correction. Never anybody else's name or private reply.
steps.note: The proof is identical on every route. A correct explanation, an honest limit, a question answered, and a correction where one was needed. Having people around and feeling confident are not requirements.

steps.title: Save your two-minute plan

fields.label: The limit I will name
fields.placeholder: Where it can be wrong, or needs checking

fields.label: The choice the listener keeps
fields.placeholder: What they decide, check, or refuse to hand over

steps.title: Can your explanation survive a question?
steps.question: Which result really shows you understand it, without needing anybody else to be available?

options.text: On any of the routes, I said the idea and its limit, answered a fair question using an example I had checked, and fixed one unclear part. I stored nobody else's details.
options.feedback: Yes. The route can be private or social. The proof is your correct explanation, your checked example, your answer, and your fix.

options.text: A made-up learner said my explanation was clear, so I did not bother checking the facts underneath.
options.feedback: Clear is not the same as correct. That route is fine, but you still have to check the core idea and answer the question yourself.

options.text: I copied a polished explanation, and never answered a question or changed a word of it.
options.feedback: Polish is not ownership. Answer one fair question and rewrite the explanation in your own words.

options.text: I taught a true idea, but I used the listener's own private situation as the example without asking.
options.feedback: The idea may be right. The method was not. Use a made-up example, and ask before using anybody's life as one.

lessons.title: The Bigger Picture
lessons.coreQuestion: AI is going to change things. How do I plan my own move instead of waiting to see what happens?
lessons.blurb: Skip the panic and the shrug. Write a three-line plan for one thing you care about, then prove it works anywhere.

steps.title: Two loud stories
steps.scenario:
Scroll for long enough and you get two stories about AI.

One says it takes every job and there is nothing you can do.

The other says it is all hype and nothing really changes.

Both are loud. Both are easy to repeat at dinner.
steps.prompt: Notice what they share. Neither one asks you to do anything this week. Which one do you catch yourself repeating?

steps.title: Panic, shrug, or something you can use?
steps.prompt: Sort each one. The useful ones are boring and specific, and they leave room for your own choices.

items.text: AI will replace everyone, so there is no point learning anything.
It is all hype. In five years we will laugh that we worried.
Most of my students will draft with AI, so 'did they write it?' stops being the useful question.
AI wants to take over creative work.
This could handle my meeting notes, so I will test it on Friday's call.

steps.reveal: A note about words. People say AI will 'decide' or 'want' to replace jobs. That is a figure of speech. It wants nothing. It has read an enormous amount of writing and guesses the words that fit next. People and companies choose where to point it. The choosing stays human, for better and worse. That includes yours.

steps.title: Plan your own move
steps.body:
The changes are uneven and hard to guess. People make choices, and those choices drive them. So build your plan from what you can actually see, not from a headline.

Four parts. One change you can point at. One thing it opens up, or one risk. One small thing you control. And a date to look again.

If you use an outside app, keep the area broad or made up. Take out your employer, school, family, town, money and anything private. What you type there leaves LearningAI.

If it searches the web, open the original pages yourself. Check the dates. Ask who benefits from the story. Anything about the future is a guess, so label it as one.

And if the doom stuff is genuinely making you anxious, talk to somebody you trust. Do not use a chat app as your only support.
steps.mistake: Waiting to see what happens. Or picking 'the world' as your area, which is far too big to act on.
steps.good: Picking one specific thing you can actually move in, like being a history teacher. Then writing the boring, doable action first.

steps.title: Draft your three lines
steps.prompt: Give me a fair, honest view of how AI might realistically affect [my area] over the next few years. Then write it as three lines. One, the most likely change, boring and specific, not a headline. Two, one real thing it opens up for me. Three, one small thing I could start this week. Be clear about what is genuinely uncertain. Do not hype it and do not doom it. About me: [one detail].
steps.note: Pick a broad area that does not identify you. Fixing bikes, looking after animals, making music, helping at a library, running a stall, learning a trade, working shifts, teaching. Do not name an employer, school, customer, or private plan. Open two original pages behind any claim about a trend, and write down what is still unclear. Then edit the plan so the action is specific, cheap, and yours to approve.

steps.title: Prove the skill is yours
steps.question: You wrote one plan. Now run the same three lines on a completely different area. If the first was work, try a hobby, your town, or somebody in your family. Which second plan passes?

options.text: Change I can see: the library is testing AI search. Opens up: faster starting points. Action: ask for a demonstration on Saturday, compare one result with the normal catalogue, and change the plan based on what I find.
options.feedback: Passes. No panic, no shrug. A stranger reading line three would know exactly what to do, on which day.

options.text: Change: parts of my hobby might get automated. Opens up: saving time. Action: follow the trend and decide later, with no source and no test.
options.feedback: Believable, but there is nothing to test. Name something you can look at, a cheap experiment, a date, and what would change your mind.

options.text: Change: an AI feature might turn up in my field. Opens up: using it right away. Action: switch it on next week without checking what it can reach.
options.feedback: Switching it on without checking what it can touch hands over control. Try it small first, and put a person's check before anything real.

lessons.title: Your Toolkit and Where to Go Next
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I get everything I learned onto one page, and prove it works on a job I have never seen?
lessons.blurb: Turn fifty lessons into one page you can open and use. Then finish.

steps.title: The week after the last lesson
steps.scenario:
It is a week from now. You open a fresh chat to write something real.

Everything you practised here is scattered across fifty lessons. Your rule. The requests that worked. Your order of doing things. Your limits.

You half remember three of them. So you type blind, like before.
steps.prompt: If everything you learned lived on ONE page you could open right now, what four things would be on it?

steps.title: A kit, not a pile of tricks
steps.body:
What you built is a way of working, not a bag of tricks. Keep it on one page.

Six things belong there.

Your rule, in one sentence. The requests you reuse. Your order of doing things. What you never hand over, and what an app may never touch. Where a person has to say yes. And how you record what you checked, and when you say AI helped.

Before an outside app sees that page, take out names, private examples, account details, confidential material, and anything about somebody else. What you type there leaves LearningAI. Test on made-up material first.

It can prepare and draft. You approve anything that gets sent, posted, paid for, deleted, or used to judge a person.

Check claims against sources you open yourself. Say that AI helped when the reader, customer, teacher or rule would want to know. Health, money, law and safety end with a professional who is answerable. In a crisis, reach a person or your local emergency service, not a chat app.
steps.mistake: Closing the course and trusting your memory to hold fifty lessons' worth of moves.
steps.good: Getting your pieces onto one saved page, then running it on something real the same day.

steps.title: Which piece is this?
steps.prompt: Sort each one. Is it a rule you keep, or a step you take? You are taking stock before you build the page.

items.text: I read and decide on anything before it goes out with my name on it.
Goal, background, limits, and what the answer should look like, for any draft.
Never paste anybody's private details into a chat.
Draft rough, ask it to pick the draft apart, rewrite in my words, check the facts, final read.
For health or money, it helps me prepare, but a real professional decides.
'Explain it back to me, then test me' when I am learning something.

steps.reveal: The lines are what keep you in charge. The moves are what get the work done. A real page has both. Lines without moves is a list of worries. Moves without lines is how people get burned.

steps.title: Build the page, then get tested on it
steps.prompt: Help me organise my one-page kit. My rule: [rule]. Requests I reuse: [requests]. My order of doing things: [steps]. What I never hand over, and what an app may never touch: [limits]. Where a person has to say yes: [stops]. How I record what I checked, and when I say AI helped: [record]. Do not add anything it may touch, and do not add private examples. Then give me one made-up job in [a broad area] that needs at least three of those pieces. Do not solve it. Ask me to name what could go wrong, what it may touch, who approves, what proof I keep, and who I would tell before I start.
steps.note: Use your own words, with anything identifying or confidential taken out. Broad areas: a community event, a repair, a game, something creative, a household plan, a job at work, or studying. Test with made-up material. It can tidy the page and set you a challenge. Your decisions and your written proof are what count.

steps.title: The last check
steps.question: You ran the made-up job using your own page. Which result means you actually passed, rather than answered a quiz?

options.text: I finished a job I had never seen using at least three pieces. I can show what it was allowed to touch, where a person said yes, one fact I checked myself, and what I would tell people in the real version.
options.feedback: That is the end of the course. You did not recall a fact. You did the skill on something new, with your own kit. Now pick where to go next: work, school, creative, everyday life, or building things. Take one step in it.

options.text: I tried three requests and the answers came out consistent, but I never said what it may touch or who approves anything.
options.feedback: Consistent answers do not show safe working. Add the least it needs, a named person who approves, and a record of what happened.

options.text: I asked it to check my own page, and accepted its report because it had links and sounded confident.
options.feedback: It can suggest checks. Its confidence and its links are not the proof. Open the sources and test the controls yourself.

options.text: I did the job and checked one claim, but next time I would let it post the result on its own.
options.feedback: The checking was strong. Posting on its own removes the place where you say yes. Keep a person's stop before anything leaves.
